World.title: Two funerals, two flashpoints: politics intrudes on mourning
World.content:
“No life is worth losing for power,” Chief Chisunka warns as funerals become flashpoints and party accuses police of standing by

Traditional leaders, a Catholic priest and an opposition party chairman have issued pointed warnings against rising political violence ahead of the 13 August general election.

Their intervention comes after two funerals in Eastern and Southern provinces this week descended into standoffs over party politics.

Chief Chisunka of the Ushi people of Luapula said no life is worth losing for the sake of power. He called on politicians to rein in their cadres before the country is set alight.

“We don’t have to lose lives just for certain people to cling to power. Peace needs to prevail because the country has been a beacon of hope,” the chief told The Mast.

He said it was unfortunate that parts of the nation were experiencing bloodshed in what he described as a Christian country. Politicians, he said, needed to sober up and tame their cadres before Zambia is drawn into wider conflict.

The Ushi traditional leader called on chiefs countrywide to rise to the occasion and denounce political violence wherever it occurs.

Catholic priest Father Gladson Phiri echoed the call. He said the church and traditional leaders are best placed to lead the fight against political violence because they deal directly with the citizens who go on to engage in political activity.

“The church and traditional leaders are the ones that should champion the fight against political violence because they usually deal with the masses who in turn engage in various political activities,” Fr Phiri said.

He said clergy and chiefs needed to engage both politicians and the electorate on the dangers of violence, warning that the country risked being set ablaze if the trend continues unchecked.

The warnings came in the same week that two funerals turned into flashpoints, illustrating how deeply campaign season has begun to intrude on ordinary community life.

In Aslot Township, Chipata District, mourners stormed out of Mgwelo Maplot Cemetery on Wednesday. The walkout came the moment a UPND official was called upon to address the gathering.

Both the ruling party and the opposition National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity had contributed toward funeral arrangements for the deceased. UPND gave K400; NRPUP reportedly covered other costs, including transport.

The solemn atmosphere shattered when director of ceremony Goldwin Soko announced that the UPND representative would give remarks. Without warning, a section of mourners rose and left the graveyard in a show of disapproval.

“When funerals are politicised and become battlegrounds, then we have a problem,” Alakwisa Jere, a Chipata-based mourner who witnessed the scene, told The Mast.

The Chipata walkout came barely a day after a similar episode in Mazabuka.

There, District Commissioner Oliver Mulomba was booed by angry residents on Tuesday and forced to abandon his speech. The crowd accused him of campaigning for President Hakainde Hichilema and the UPND at a funeral.

Mr Mulomba had to leave the scene to avoid possible harm.

Jere warned that the Chipata and Mazabuka incidents were a sign of what could unfold as campaigning intensifies in the final stretch before polling day. Leaders from both UPND and opposition parties have since appealed for calm, urging cadres and officials to keep politics out of funerals and other community gatherings.

Separately, Leadership Movement national chairperson David Kalumba accused the Zambia Police Service of failing to act against known perpetrators of political violence.

“Police officers have become spectators of violence,” he said in a statement.

He said his party had campaigned throughout the country encouraging people to reject violence and demand accountability, but that police had “betrayed people it is supposed to protect by failing to stop violence.”

Kalumba said no one should celebrate the destruction of public and private property currently taking place in parts of the country at the hands of political cadres. Zambians, he warned, must reject political violence at all costs, because the aftermath would be difficult to rebuild from.

He stressed that his own party was not a violent movement but a pro-poor organisation focused on building a Zambia with equal job and business opportunities for all.

“Our people have told us that all they want is peace, unity and development, and that is the message we are preaching,” he said.

The Leadership Movement chairman said his party had learnt a great deal on the 2026 campaign trail. Poverty, underdevelopment and lack of opportunity, he said, remain a disease afflicting many communities, particularly in rural areas he accused previous leadership of excluding from the national development agenda.

“Our people in rural areas need development but they cannot see it because previous leadership have excluded them from national development agenda,” Kalumba said.

He pledged that, if voted into office, his party would open access to rural development, working toward better roads, schools, markets, hospitals and clinics for rural communities.

Kalumba said the rural population should remain the main focus for the next five years, noting that the rural vote is larger than the urban vote on the current voter register.

Taken together, the warnings from traditional and religious leaders and the accusations levelled by the Leadership Movement chairman paint a picture of mounting anxiety over the tone of the campaign’s final fortnight. Community leaders are now openly worried that political competition could spill into the kind of bloodshed Zambia has largely avoided in recent electoral cycles.

World.title: Africa: Africa's Energy Crossroads: What Namibia's Rise and South Africa's Debate Mean for the Continent
World.content:
guest column

Africa stands at one of the most consequential moments in its modern economic history.

From the offshore oil discoveries of Namibia to the natural gas reserves of Mozambique, from Angola's mature petroleum industry to Senegal and Mauritania's emergence as new energy producers, the continent is witnessing the birth of a new energy era. Uganda is advancing towards commercial oil production, Ghana continues to build on its offshore success, while countries such as Kenya, Tanzania and Somalia continue exploring their hydrocarbon potential.

Yet beneath these diverse national stories lies a single continental question: Can Africa convert its abundant natural resources into lasting prosperity?

The answer will depend less on what lies beneath the ground than on what exists above it—strong institutions, sound governance, policy certainty and visionary leadership.



In that context, the contrasting experiences of Namibia and South Africa offer valuable lessons not only for Southern Africa, but for every African nation seeking to attract investment while safeguarding its long-term national interests.

For decades, Namibia and South Africa have shared more than a border. They have shared history, infrastructure, trade and access to one of the world's most promising offshore geological formations—the Orange Basin.

Today, however, their energy trajectories are beginning to diverge.

Namibia is rapidly emerging as one of the world's newest oil-producing nations. Successive offshore discoveries have attracted billions of dollars in investment from international energy companies, transforming the country into one of Africa's most closely watched investment destinations.

Its success is about far more than oil.

It demonstrates that investors are drawn not only to geological potential, but also to countries that provide regulatory clarity, institutional stability, efficient decision-making and confidence that major projects can progress within predictable timeframes.

South Africa, by contrast, possesses considerable offshore hydrocarbon potential and one of Africa's most sophisticated industrial economies. Yet development has progressed more slowly as policymakers, regulators, industry and civil society continue debating the balance between environmental protection, legislative reform and investment certainty.

Neither approach should be caricatured.

Environmental stewardship remains essential. Africa cannot afford development that compromises its oceans, biodiversity or future generations. Equally, prolonged uncertainty can discourage investment, delay economic opportunities and shift capital towards jurisdictions where regulatory pathways are perceived to be more predictable.

This is not simply South Africa's challenge.

It is a policy dilemma confronting governments across Africa.

Whether in Nigeria as it reforms its petroleum sector, Mozambique as it develops its LNG industry, Senegal and Mauritania as they enter production, Uganda as it prepares to export oil, or emerging exploration markets elsewhere on the continent, governments are grappling with the same fundamental question: how can Africa attract investment while ensuring that its natural wealth delivers lasting benefits for its people?

The countries that answer that question successfully will shape Africa's economic future.

Global investment capital is increasingly selective.

Energy companies compare opportunities in Namibia not only with South Africa or Angola, but also with Guyana, Brazil, Suriname, Norway, Qatar and other energy-producing jurisdictions. Investment decisions are influenced by regulatory certainty, governance standards, fiscal stability, infrastructure, local skills and the confidence that projects can move efficiently from discovery to production.

Africa therefore competes not merely within itself—it competes with the world.

That reality should encourage greater continental cooperation rather than rivalry.

The African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) presents an opportunity to think beyond national borders. Imagine a Southern African energy and industrial corridor connecting Angola's petroleum expertise, Namibia's offshore discoveries, South Africa's financial and manufacturing capabilities, Mozambique's natural gas resources, Botswana's logistics strengths and the engineering talent found across the region.

Such integration could stimulate local manufacturing, strengthen African supply chains, develop world-class technical skills, increase regional value addition and create hundreds of thousands of high-quality jobs.

Instead of exporting raw resources and importing finished products, Africa could increasingly build, process, manufacture and innovate at home.

This is ultimately the continent's greatest opportunity.

Oil and gas should not be viewed as ends in themselves. They are catalysts that can finance economic diversification, renewable energy, scientific research, education, healthcare, infrastructure and industrial development.

History offers Africa both inspiration and warning.

Some resource-rich nations transformed natural wealth into broad-based prosperity through sound governance and long-term planning. Others became cautionary examples of missed opportunity, institutional weakness and overdependence on commodity exports.

The choice remains Africa's to make.

Namibia's emergence deserves celebration because it demonstrates what is possible when natural opportunity is matched by policy confidence and institutional credibility. South Africa's experience equally offers valuable lessons about the importance of balancing environmental responsibility with regulatory efficiency and investment certainty.

Neither country represents the entire African story.

Together, however, they illuminate choices confronting governments from Dakar to Dar es Salaam, from Kampala to Windhoek, from Accra to Maputo.

Ultimately, Africa's future will not be determined by the quantity of oil beneath its seabed or minerals beneath its soil.

Close 

It will be determined by the quality of its institutions, the consistency of its policies, the transparency of its governance and the courage of leaders willing to make decisions that balance today's opportunities with tomorrow's responsibilities.

The race for Africa's energy future has already begun.

Those nations that embrace cooperation over competition, certainty over indecision and long-term national vision over short-term political calculation will not simply attract investment—they will help define Africa's next chapter of economic transformation.

The question is no longer whether Africa possesses the resources to prosper.

The question is whether Africa will build the institutions capable of turning those resources into a lasting legacy for generations to come.

------------------

Daniel Makokera is a renowed media personality who has worked as journalist, television anchor, producer and conference presenter for over 20 years. Throughout his career as presenter and anchor, he has travelled widely across the continent and held exclusive interviews with some of Africa's most illustrious leaders. These include former UN Secretary General Kofi Annan, former South African presidents Nelson Mandela and Thabo Mbeki, former Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi, Zimbabwean Prime Minister Morgan Tsvangirai and presidents Robert Mugabe of Zimbabwe and Joseph Kabila of the Democratic Republic of the Congo. He currently is the CEO of Pamuzinda Productions based in South Africa.

World.title: Africa: Cotton to Cloth - The Story Africa Has Always Needed to Tell
World.content:
editorial

Africa grows more than half of the world's finest long-staple cotton. It earns less than three percent of what that cotton is eventually worth. This is not a trade problem. It is a narrative problem — and allAfrica is setting out to fix it.

There is a number that explains much of what is wrong with how the world finances Africa. It is not a trade figure or a debt ratio. It is an annual cost — up to $4.2 billion — the amount by which negative media stereotypes inflate African sovereign borrowing costs every single year. The story the world reads about Africa costs Africa, concretely, in higher interest rates and slower capital flows.

allAfrica has spent close to 3 decades building the infrastructure to change that story. Eight million articles in archive. A network of 140+ media partners spanning every corner of the continent. Direct distribution reaching tens of millions of decision-makers globally through Bloomberg, Dow Jones/Factiva, Thomson Reuters, Moody's Analytics/NewsEdge, LexisNexis, Syndigate & Tagaday (Europe). We are, in the most literal sense, the channel through which Africa's story reaches the people who price African risk.

Cotton to Cloth is the moment we unlock the full power of the infrastructure we have built over the years.



"The gap between raw commodity and finished product is not a production gap. It is a perception gap — and journalism, data, and storytelling can close it." — Amadou Mahtar Ba · Co-Founder, allAfrica Global Media

The initiative

Beginning June 2026 and running through December, allAfrica launches its most sustained and investment-grade editorial programme to date — a dedicated hub on all its platforms covering every dimension of Africa's cotton-to-cloth transformation, built on the conviction that Africa's cotton story — told well, distributed broadly, and anchored in data — can measurably shift how the world's capital allocators think about the continent.

The story begins in the field. West African cotton is among the finest on earth — long-staple, clean, commanding a premium on international markets. It leaves the continent as raw fibre. It returns as finished garments at twenty, thirty, sometimes fifty times the price. The countries that grow the raw material that clothes the world are rarely named as manufacturers. That is the gap this initiative addresses, one story at a time.

What you will find on this hub



This page is the entry point for all allAfrica content on this initiative. Over the coming months, it will grow into the most comprehensive English and French editorial resource on African cotton industrialisation available anywhere online — spanning original journalism, investor intelligence, documentary storytelling, policy analysis, and voices from across the continent and its diaspora.

Original long-form journalism. A sustained monthly publication series going deep on the economics, the geography, the people, and the policy architecture of Africa's cotton transformation — written to the standard that institutional investors, policymakers, and informed readers require. Evidence-based, rigorous, told from the inside.

Investor-grade data and intelligence. A major annual data publication mapping Africa's cotton processing investment landscape, a live deal tracker updated monthly, and sector intelligence briefs — all structured for capital markets audiences and distributed through allAfrica's global institutional wire network.

Policy voices and thought leadership. Commissioned essays, opinion pieces, and in-depth interviews bringing African ministers, industrialists, economists, and sector leaders directly to the audiences that shape policy and move capital — wire-distributed to the financial press and reaching Bloomberg, Factiva, LexisNexis, and beyond.

Documentary and multimedia storytelling. Original documentary features, a podcast series, and data-driven visual content placing human faces and real places at the centre of the industrial story — from the floor of a processing zone to the hands of a cooperative farmer, the cotton-to-cloth story in full depth and colour.

Close 

Youth and diaspora voices. A continent-wide storytelling contest inviting contributors from across Africa and the African diaspora to tell the cotton-to-cloth story in their own words. The next generation of African economic narrators, brought in from the first day.

Live events and convenings. A virtual roundtable, a physical exhibition at the allAfrica Media Leaders Summit, and allAfrica's presence at major African institutional forums throughout the year — taking this story from screen to room.

Follow the story



Everything on this hub is free. Every article, data release, documentary, and podcast will be published in both English and French — because the cotton-to-cloth story is as much a Francophone African story as it is an Anglophone one, and allAfrica serves the full continent.

Subscribe and receive each new publication directly in your inbox from launch day.

World.title: Uganda: HIV Injection Is Not a Vaccine, Experts Warn
World.content:
Kampala — Experts have urged those who already received their first injection of the twice-yearly HIV preventing drug Lenacapavir to consider using combination prevention options, warning that the game changer injection is not a vaccine.

The initial recipients of the drug that has since had a lot of demand countrywide are set to receive their second dose in October and Dr Vincent Bagambe, the Policy Planning and Strategic Manager at the Uganda AIDS Commission says for those who access it, they should be keen on receiving their next dose on the prescribed dates if they are to maintain optimal drug levels in their blood.

Bagambe says that with the injection now part of the prevention tools in the country, they hope to cut the 37,000 new infections recorded yearly to less than 10,000 by 2030, which will all depend on how compliant people be to maintain the required drug levels in their blood to guarantee protection.

At the launch of the prevention option in April, Uganda had received 19,200 doses supplied across 103 health facilities across the country. The main clients targeted for the drug include people at highest risk of infection such as sex workers, couples in discordant relationships, fisherfolk and pregnant women engaging in risky behavior among others. But reports by the Ministry of Health show that the drug was accessed by those not listed as high risk as demand surpassed available supplies.



Asked about supplies for those who will soon need the second dose, Dr Herbert Kadama who coordinates Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis (PrEP) at the Ministry of Health said sixty - percent of the facilities that received the first batch have now received second batches.

Kadama explains that the facilities received the second batches earlier than scheduled because the doses were running out in two to three weeks and yet at the beginning, they had thought they would be supplying every two months.

Meanwhile, the country expects a top-up consignment of another 19,200 doses donation.

In an earlier interview with URN, Dr Peter Mudiope who heads HIV Prevention in the ministry this consignment was initially expected to arrive in the country in June only to be informed by the manufacturer Gilead Sciences that this couldn't happen due to shortages of a tablet that complements the injection, also called the loading dose.

Mudiope says that as calls for more doses continue and the valid need for people to comply on the prevention treatment, government cannot do much to avail the game changer drug for now. He says the current price of Lenacapivir is still too high to be afforded by the government. At 28,000 dollars per dose, the official says Uganda can for now only count on more donations expected from Global Fund and the American government to guarantee availability.

Close 

With supplies not yet guaranteed, Mudiope says the public should continue relying on other prevention options such as condoms, Pre and Post Exposure Prophylaxis tablets and being faithful as they are equally scientifically tested and confirmed to prevent HIV infection.

However, a study conducted by Makerere University School of Public Health in which they assessed access to HIV prevention services found use of key prevention options low.

According to results of this study which were released on Wednesday, researchers found only 24 percent of female sex workers and injection drug users, who are also a high at-risk group used PEP in the last three months. Seventy-six percent reported to have not used the prevention option despite knowledge of where to access it.

In terms prevalence, while national prevalence currently stands at 4.9 percent, among sex workers and injection drug users, HIV prevalence is high at 30 percent and 17 percent respectively.

Ideally, Kadama says such groups are the ones targeted as a top priority for Lenacapavir.

World.title: East Africa: U.S. Senators Urge Rubio to Address Impact of Ebola Outbreak on Women

press release

WASHINGTON — Yesterday, U.S. Senators Jeanne Shaheen (D-NH), Ranking Member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, and Lisa Murkowski (R-AK) sent a letter to Secretary of State Marco Rubio urging the State Department to take swift action to protect women and infants from the deadly impact of the Ebola outbreak in eastern Africa. The Senators called on the Trump Administration to promptly use congressionally appropriated funds for voluntary family planning programming to distribute already purchased family planning commodities and back the UN Population Fund’s (UNFPA) health clinics operating in the region.

In the letter, the Senators emphasized the catastrophic toll of Ebola on pregnant women and warned that conflict and displacement in Ituri and North Kivu—in addition to increases in gender-based and sexual violence and transactional and survival sex—are exacerbating the outbreak.

“Ebola during pregnancy is catastrophic, with a nearly 100 percent fetal loss rate and catastrophic maternal mortality risk due to severe hemorrhaging. By providing women with the option to voluntarily prevent unplanned pregnancies and to protect themselves from transmission of the virus and have access to clinics, the United States can prevent further deaths of women and the cruel and certain death of any fetus exposed to the virus,” wrote the Senators.

“The inclusion of family planning in the U.S. response to the Ebola virus, including condoms and hormonal contraceptive methods, post-rape care and lifesaving anti-hemorrhage maternal health medicines is paramount. Congress, on a bipartisan basis, supports voluntary family planning programs because such programs support families and reduce maternal and infant death rates. In East Africa right now, access to family planning is essential to protecting women and babies and to reducing viral transmission,” continued the Senators.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

“The rapid spread of the virus, with more than 2,000 confirmed cases and 796 confirmed deaths as of this week in the DRC, leaves no time for delay in providing all possible interventions to save lives and prevent the transmission of the virus. The cost of United States response is approaching $1 billion. Investment now in voluntary family planning is fiscally rational in addition to being morally urgent,” concluded the Senators.

Full text of the letter is available HERE and provided below.

Dear Secretary Rubio,

We write to urge the State Department to take swift action to address the devastating impact of the Ebola outbreak in eastern Africa on women and infants by utilizing funding provided by Congress for voluntary family planning programming, to distribute already purchased family planning commodities and supporting the UN Population Fund’s (UNFPA) health clinics in the region.

By providing women with the option to voluntarily prevent unplanned pregnancies and to protect themselves from transmission of the virus and have access to clinics, the United States can prevent further deaths of women and the cruel and certain death of any fetus exposed to the virus.

During the Ebola outbreak in West Africa from 2014-2016, maternal mortality rose an estimated 75%. The staggering increase in maternal mortality was a result of the Ebola virus, as well as pregnant women forgoing antenatal and attended delivery care because of fear of contracting the virus at health clinics.

Currently, conflict and displacement are exacerbating the Ebola outbreak with spikes in gender-based and sexual violence in Ituri and North Kivu, as well as an increase in transactional and survival sex. Access to voluntary family planning counseling and supplies is critical to protect the lives of women and babies and to control the spread of the virus.

The inclusion of family planning in the U.S. response to the Ebola virus, including condoms and hormonal contraceptive methods, post-rape care and lifesaving anti-hemorrhage maternal health medicines is paramount. Congress, on a bipartisan basis, supports voluntary family planning programs because such programs support families and reduce maternal and infant death rates. In East Africa right now, access to family planning is essential to protecting women and babies and to reducing viral transmission. We urge you to utilize the $608 million in international family planning funding included in the Fiscal Year 2026 Appropriations bill and to distribute the remaining $1.7 million in already purchased family planning commodities in storage in Geel, Belgium which we understand will otherwise be destroyed.

We also ask that you issue a humanitarian exemption to support UNFPA's sexual and reproductive health programming in affected areas. UNFPA is already operational across 29 health zones in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and in Uganda; emergency contributions would be deployed immediately through an existing, proven delivery system with no ramp-up delay. Providing sexual and reproductive health support to women is not a parallel track alongside the Ebola response: it is the Ebola response for the 642,000 women of reproductive age - including an estimated 37,820 pregnant women - in the affected areas.

The rapid spread of the virus, with more than 2,000 confirmed cases and 796 confirmed deaths as of this week in the DRC, leaves no time for delay in providing all possible interventions to save lives and prevent the transmission of the virus. World.title: Nigeria: South African Singer Tyla Cancels Lagos Performance Amid Xenophobia Backlash
World.content:
South African singer Tyla has removed Lagos from the schedule of her upcoming APop world tour following online backlash from some Nigerians over renewed reports of xenophobic attacks against Nigerians in South Africa.

The Grammy-winning artiste unveiled the dates for her world tour on Monday, with the initial itinerary including a Lagos concert scheduled for December 22, alongside stops across Europe, North America and South Africa.

However, the announcement sparked heated reactions on Nigerian social media, where several users questioned the decision to host the singer amid reports of fresh xenophobic violence targeting Nigerians in South Africa.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The controversy revived long-standing tensions between both countries, with some social media users calling for a boycott of the Lagos concert.

Others argued that entertainment should not be linked to diplomatic disputes and maintained that musicians should not be held responsible for political or societal conflicts.

A number of public figures also weighed in on the debate.

Media personality Do2dtun questioned the promoters behind the planned Lagos show, while activist and former presidential candidate Omoyele Sowore urged Nigerians to channel their frustrations toward political leaders rather than the artiste.

Neither Tyla nor her management publicly addressed the criticism.

However, checks by VANGUARD showed that Lagos has been removed from the list of tour venues on the official ticketing platform.

The previously announced December 22 show in Nigeria no longer appears among the available dates.

The updated schedule now lists only the remaining international stops, including performances across Europe, North America and two South African shows in Cape Town on January 4 and Johannesburg on January 9.

Tyla has not announced whether the Lagos concert was cancelled permanently or if it could be rescheduled at a later date.

World.title: Israeli orphans of fallen heroes find pride, connection on US journey

Twenty-eight children from across Israel who lost a parent killed while serving in the country's security forces participated in a three-week delegation to North America as part of the IDF Widows & Orphans Organization's annual Bar/Bat Mitzvah program.

The journey began last month in Chicago, where the children spent a weekend with host families before traveling to Camp Chi in Wisconsin for nearly a week of activities with American kids. They then continued to New York City, where they visited Times Square and saw The Lion King on Broadway, before heading to New Jersey. For many, it was their first visit to the United States.

FREED HOSTAGE ROM BRASLAVSKI DETAILS ABUSE, STARVATION DURING 738 DAYS IN GAZA CAPTIVITY

"Everything is planned very carefully. The Lion King, for instance, is more than a Broadway show for them. It’s the story of an orphan who is able to honor his father’s memory and move forward because of the support of his friends. Nothing about this trip is accidental. It is deliberately designed to give them as powerful and meaningful an experience as possible," Daniel Elbaum, executive director of the IDF Widows & Orphans Organization, told Fox News Digital.

With the United States home to the world’s largest Jewish population outside Israel, the trip gave the children an opportunity to meet people from diverse backgrounds and levels of religious observance while, for many, experiencing international travel independently for the first time — which Elbaum said reflects their entry into the covenant with the Jewish people in a tangible and meaningful way.

Although the trip was not designed as an initiative to combat antisemitism, Elbaum said fostering a strong Jewish identity, pride in Israel and solidarity with its people are among the most important ways to help American Jews confront the world's oldest hatred.

"As much as I think we are doing something important for these Israeli children, whose families have paid the highest price for Israel, what we are doing for the American children is almost as important in giving them a sense of pride and connection they might not otherwise experience," he added.

INSIDE ISRAEL'S MISSION TO TRAIN CIVILIANS TO STOP THE NEXT OCT 7-LIKE TERROR ATTACK

Founded in 1991, the IDF Widows & Orphans Organization supports more than 18,000 widows, widowers and orphans through assistance programs, rehabilitation, advocacy and legislative efforts. Since the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023 massacre and the ensuing war, 359 widows and widowers — including 48 pregnant widows — and 910 new orphans have joined Israel’s circle of bereavement.

Among this year’s participants was 11½-year-old Tal Goldstein-Almog from Kibbutz Kfar Aza, who was taken hostage to Gaza with his mother and two siblings on Oct. 7 and held for 51 days. His father, Nadav, and sister Yam, an IDF soldier, were murdered during the attack.

Tal did not tell the other children he had been held captive until one evening, when he felt ready to share his experience.

"It’s not hard to tell people, but it’s not easy either. Once you’ve said it, you don’t know how others will react or treat you. That night, it felt safe to open up, and nothing has changed in the way they treat me since," he told Fox News Digital.

The trip was Tal's first extended journey without his family. He learned about the program from a friend from the kibbutz who also participated.

ISRAEL'S NEW EXHIBIT EXPOSES YEARS OF HAMAS TERRORIST PLANNING BEFORE OCT 7 MASSACRE

"Now that I came, I think I will continue taking part in these things after meeting new kids, feeling comfortable around them and understanding that we experienced the same things," he said.

Tal said that since Oct. 7, the connections in his life have helped him maintain a sense of normalcy.

"My motto is that life is always going to continue," he added. "It feels refreshing to come to a new country and experience fun things here."

Shadan Knefiss first participated in the program as an IDF orphan and has since returned as a counselor, supporting the next generation of bereaved children. A member of Israel’s Druze community, she also joined the delegation to help translate for participants whose first language is Arabic.

"I met a lot of people here who don’t know about the Druze. We serve the country, we love our country, and we even die for it. We pay the same price as everyone else. Most terrorists in Israel are Arab, but because we speak Arabic and serve our country, it’s a bit of a twist," she told Fox News Digital.



Shadan became an orphan at the age of three. Her father, a Border Police officer stationed in Jerusalem, transferred to northern Israel after her brother was born with a serious skin condition so he could be closer to the family. He was killed in a car accident during his first shift there.

"This program helped me in so many ways throughout my life. The people around me have not all lost their father, so sometimes I can’t relate to them. Sometimes I want to share how I feel, but they don’t understand. This program made me feel comfortable talking about things I can’t discuss with people in my everyday life," she said.

Noor, 13, was one of three participants whom Shadan helped during the trip. His father, Yosef Saleh, served in the IDF before joining the Israel Police, where he was killed in the line of duty in 2013.

Noor told Fox News Digital that it was his first trip to the United States. "My message to other children like us is to go on trips, meet new kids and make new friends," Noor said.

JOHANNESBURG: The U.S. is beating China in a high-tech trade war over data centers in a fierce battle being waged across Africa.

Major new deals have been engineered in a public-private partnership between the Trump administration and U.S. companies in Africa, while States across the U.S. clamp down on the centers over their massive reliance on electricity.

The administration’s Bureau of African Affairs has reported it has worked on 37 commercial transactions that have closed since the beginning of President Donald Trump’s second term — representing $25.67 billion in total value, with more still being reported.

RESOURCE-RICH NATION PRAISES US TIES AMID WASHINGTON-BEIJING CRITICAL MINERALS RACE

Data centers are at the heart of today's global economy — fueling the massive demand for AI and hosting everything from video streaming to housing cloud networks.

In Lesotho, with U.S. help, an American company has won a $6.2 billion deal for a data center and hydropower plant. It is the largest transaction in this Southern African country’s history.

In Gabon, the U.S. Embassy helped win $600 million in business for American companies in 2025. And this year, the embassy in this central African country has assisted in securing a $100 million contract to supply two data centers and a gas-to-power plant, in the face of strong competition from China.

Assistant Secretary of State for African Affairs, Frank Garcia, told Fox News Digital, "Under President Trump’s leadership, the United States is assisting U.S. companies to find new markets and flourish in Africa."

The main strategic competitor in Africa is China. While American goods traded with Africa last year were valued at $83.4 billion by the Office of the United States Trade Representative, Beijing’s General Administration of Customs claimed bilateral trade between China and Africa reached $348 billion for the same period.

But Garcia called out China for giving African countries a raw deal, saying "there are others (notably China) that trap, coerce and undermine. The choice to me is clear — partner with the United States for prosperity."

To drive this initiative, the State Department, through the Bureau of African Affairs, launched the Commercial Diplomacy Strategy in early 2025, with Garcia telling Fox News Digital the U.S. "is working worldwide to advance a level playing field for U.S. companies and address disparities in trade practices."

The playing fields in Lesotho are not level: Geographically because this is a mountain kingdom. Financially because China is historically deeply entrenched in life there. Beijing has dropped all tariffs on Lesotho’s exports. Payments between the two countries have been simplified, with Lesothans able to bank directly with the State-owned Industrial and Commercial Bank of China.

Beijing has canceled debt on major projects in Lesotho, and among other major projects is building a new fire station, a solar power plant and even completed a police fingerprint examination laboratory.

CHINA IS BUILDING AN AI WAR MACHINE. WASHINGTON MUST WAKE UP BEFORE IT’S TOO LATE

This makes it all the more remarkable that, with the administration’s help, primarily through the local embassy, U.S. company Convalt Energy has secured a $6.2 billion agreement with the government of Lesotho.

Garcia told Fox News Digital that the "project includes a 1,200MW pumped-storage hydropower facility and a 900MW AI data center, increasing Lesotho's electricity generation capacity by approximately 1,600% and transforming the country into a net exporter of electricity. The project is expected to generate approximately $2 billion in U.S. energy equipment exports."

Convalt Energy’s President & CEO, Hari Achuthan, told Fox News Digital how U.S. companies such as his are beating China on their traditional turf "American companies can compete successfully by innovating faster, integrating hardware and software, and remaining intensely focused on the needs of the end customer."

A new data center, Achuthan believes, is not only at the heart of the project, but is essential for any country’s growth. "The next major cycle of economic growth will increasingly be driven by artificial intelligence, digital infrastructure and the energy systems required to support them. AI cannot scale without physical infrastructure. Every data center requires reliable power, water, fiber connectivity, land, cooling systems and resilient transmission infrastructure."

"The Trump administration’s emphasis on trade and private-sector investment, rather than relying primarily on grant funding, is closely aligned with our approach in Africa," Achuthan continued. "In Lesotho, we are pursuing a commercially sustainable infrastructure platform built around long-term investment, bilateral trade with a durable, sustainable operating business."

"At the same time," Achuthan added, "the project can create meaningful economic benefits in the United States. Convalt’s U.S. manufacturing facilities are being developed to serve domestic customers as well as international markets, particularly Africa, where demand for power, manufacturing capacity and digital infrastructure is growing rapidly."

The construction of two data centers is part of the $100 million deal Assistant Secretary Garcia says administration officials have helped American company Cybastion secure. Garcia added, "notably, the U.S. company prevailed over Huawei (a Chinese company) in a direct competition for the project."

Cybastion CEO Dr. Thierry Wandji believes U.S. companies can and are now coming to the fore. Earlier this month the U.S. embassy in the Ivory Coast confirmed an even larger deal for Cybastion. The $170 million contract will bring a data center, government digitalization platform and a cutting-edge border surveillance system to this West African country.

Wandji told Fox News Digital, "We believe we are the better option compared to other global competitors. Cybastion brings a unique understanding of the African context and local business environments."

"Africa has some of the world's fastest-growing economies," Wandji continued. "Across the continent, countries are prioritizing sovereign data centers, modernizing their government services through digitalization, and digital workforce development as part of their national development plans.

"The U.S. tech sector offers global competitiveness unparalleled to any country in the world," Wandji added. "We deliver innovation, transparency and accountability in our business offerings, while creating new markets for U.S. companies."

Convalt’s Achuthan told Fox News Digital what’s working for U.S. business in Africa, "American companies must clearly communicate the value of quality, transparency, safety, responsible business practices and long-term community partnership. Competing solely on price is not enough going forward. Companies from the United States should compete on performance, reliability, innovation, institutional trust and the ability to create sustainable local economic benefits."

World.title: Inside the behemoth Smithsonian museum network drawing fire from the Trump administration
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

The Smithsonian Institution, whose museums in Washington, D.C. have come under fire from conservatives and President Donald Trump over what they describe as increasingly left-wing messaging, is the world's largest museum complex, comprising a sprawling network that spans the country and influences millions of people each year.

Founded in 1846 with funds from the will of British scientist James Smithson, who never visited the United States but left his fortune to establish an institution "for the increase and diffusion of knowledge," the Smithsonian steadily grew from a single museum into the world's largest museum, education and research complex.

Today, the Smithsonian owns or leases nearly 700 facilities across eight states, Washington, D.C., and Panama, encompassing roughly 13.6 million square feet of museums, laboratories, archives, warehouses, research stations and support facilities.

The organization now houses more than 157 million artifacts and specimens, operates 21 museums along with the National Zoo and 14 education and research centers, maintains 21 libraries, and partners with more than 200 affiliate museums and cultural institutions nationwide.

TRUMP ORDERS SIGNS OUTSIDE SMITHSONIAN MUSEUM AMID ROW OVER ITS DEPICTION OF AMERICAN HISTORY

Visitors see only a fraction of the Smithsonian’s overall collection. Roughly 99% of the Smithsonian's more than 157 million artifacts and specimens are kept in storage facilities, laboratories and archives, where they are preserved and studied by researchers.

The Smithsonian as a whole welcomes over 30 million in-person visitors each year, while its educational resources and digital platforms reach millions more. The institution operates on an annual budget of more than $1 billion.

The Smithsonian isn't just a museum operator, it's effectively a national education and research institution that has a vast reach across school campuses nationwide as it helps shape the educational experience of the nation’s students.

GOP LAWMAKER DEMANDS ANSWERS AFTER SMITHSONIAN CHIEF URGED MOVING BEYOND 'AMERICA FIRST MENTALITY'

Through initiatives like the Smithsonian Learning Lab and Smithsonian Science Education Center, the institution provides millions of free lesson plans, classroom activities, virtual field trips and other educational resources used by teachers and students nationwide. It also offers professional development for educators and educational programming that extends well beyond its museums.

On college campuses, the Smithsonian is actively involved in partnering with schools across the country on internships, fellowships, research collaborations and joint academic programs which put the organization in touch with thousands of undergraduate, graduate and postdoctoral students each year.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Earlier this month, the White House released a sweeping report warning about an alleged infiltration of leftist politics inside the Smithsonian, a report an expert told Fox News Digital is an example of the "long march through the institutions" that socialist and communist activists have been pushing in the United States for decades.

"That shift from history to activism is clearly documented in this report. Anthea Hartig, NMAH’s director since 2019, has explicitly stated that she sees history as a ‘prime tool of social justice’ and one of her roles as connecting ‘research and scholarship to activism and advocacy,’" the White House report stated.

Last week, President Trump ordered his administration to install signs outside the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History directing visitors to what the White House describes as "accurate" information about the nation's past, guaranteeing that the controversy over the Smithsonian's cultural influence will remain a topic of conversation for months to come.

HOUSE REPUBLICANS AIM TO TURN DEMOCRATIC CIVIL WAR INTO MIDTERM WEAPON

"I try not to waste my time on worry. I try to take action. So I just say very clearly, 'That's not me and that's not us, and this is why that's not us, and that's why this is not me.' And I fight back against it," Suozzi said. "And there are a lot of Democrats who say, 'Oh, if you look at it, it's just a very small percentage in very deep-blue seats. And it's not that big a deal.' I think that's wrong to just discount it like that. I think you just come out head-on, and take it on and say, 'These guys are wrong. We've got nothing to do with them.'"

100 DAY SPRINT TO THE MIDTERMS KICKS OFF AS REPUBLICANS AND DEMOCRATS CLASH FOR CONTROL ACROSS THE COUNTRY

Suozzi himself is part of an ever-shrinking group of moderates on both sides of the aisle. He's also co-chair of the bipartisan Problem Solvers Caucus, which is dedicated to finding legislative solutions that both parties can get behind.

The New York Democrat is one of Republicans' top targets in the coming midterm elections, and his November victory would be key to Democrats taking back control of the House. Suozzi's district, anchored in the wealthy Long Island suburbs outside of New York City, was won by President Donald Trump in 2024.

He told Fox News Digital that Democrats should not focus on running against Trump the person, but rather argue about his specific policy actions.

"Your grocery prices are higher, your fuel prices are high, your health insurance costs are higher. Your energy bill is higher. Your kids can't buy a house — all these different factors. And that's happening because of this administration," Suozzi argued. "I think it should be less about Trump himself. You know, when I say it should be a referendum on Trump, it should be a referendum on this administration's performance addressing the things in your life."

Meanwhile, Republicans have argued that a Democrat-controlled House will embolden the party's socialist wing to take control and push policies that are unpopular with Americans.

In the Empire State, for example, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, a self-described democratic socialist, has become a prominent boogeyman for the right.

Suozzi said the tactic "would be effective" if he had not distanced himself from the socialist's policy platform early on.

"He's a very smart guy, he's very charismatic," Suozzi said. "I just fundamentally disagree with his positions on things."

But it's not enough to speak out against the socialist left, Suozzi warned.

"I started a thing called The Promise to America, where I've got now 10 members of Congress signed onto it. We're in the process of getting 200 state and local officials," he said. "We've identified 10 candidates, Democratic candidates, to sign the pledge that says 'We're capitalist, not socialist. We're for safety, not lawlessness. We're proud, not ashamed of America, and we're mainstream, we're not extreme.' So we've just got to organize, we've got to do the work necessary."

World.title: U.S. agrees to pause attacks on Iran subject to ‘rapidly’ making deal, Trump says
World.content:
The U.S. has agreed to pause attacks on Iran, President Donald Trump said Saturday, amid what he said were the “perimeters of a deal” being agreed upon, which would include the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz.

“We have just been asked by Iran, and other Middle Eastern Countries, to hold off any attack in that the perimeters of a deal has been agreed to,” Trump said in a post on Truth Social. “This would include the Immediate, Complete, and Total OPENING OF THE HORMUZ STRAIT, and an end to Iran’s nuclear threat.”

The president said the U.S. was “locked and loaded and ready to go” against Iran but that he agreed to cancel attacks “subject to being able to rapidly make a DEAL.”

He added that Israel, the U.S. partner in the war with Iran, “joins me in this commitment.”

“Get to work, everybody, and get it DONE,” Trump said of a possible new agreement.

The statement came after the State Department on Saturday urged Americans across the Middle East to consider leaving the region or be prepared to depart on short notice. It also warned of flight disruptions and security risks as the conflict with Iran appeared to be escalating.

Trump earlier threatened Iran with additional attacks, saying Friday that the U.S. will be “hitting them very hard,” while Iran has vowed to “punish” the U.S. and both nations traded what some U.S. officials described as “heavy” strikes.

“Americans currently in the Middle East should exercise caution and heightened vigilance and should be prepared for flight cancellations, periodic airspace closures, and potential travel disruptions,” the State Department said Saturday. “Some airlines in the region have postponed resumption of earlier flight schedules; others have cancelled some routes. Americans in the region should consider departing, or be prepared to depart should there be escalation.”

The State Department also urged Americans to reconsider travel bans to or through the region.

Residents inspect the damage caused by Israeli airstrikes last night on residential buildings in the Safatawi area of Gaza on Aug. 1. Ahmad Hasaballah / Getty Images

The warning was distributed through U.S. embassies in the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Iraq, Israel, Jordan, Kuwait, Lebanon, Oman, Qatar and Saudi Arabia.

The agency posted a nearly identical statement earlier this month, but that bulletin did not urge Americans to prepare to leave the Middle East or to reconsider upcoming trips, reflecting Washington’s growing concern that the conflict could widen.

On Saturday, the Kuwait Army said its air defense systems intercepted drone attacks from Iran.

“Kuwaiti air defenses are currently engaging hostile drone attacks following the Iranian aggression. The General Staff of the Army notes that any explosions heard are a result of air defense systems intercepting the hostile attacks,” the army said.

Two days ago, the U.S. military confirmed it had executed a “heavy wave of strikes” on Iran, hours after Fox News reported that the president in a phone call had vowed to “beat the f-----g s--- out of” the country.

Trump has grown increasingly exasperated with the state of the war, one Trump ally told NBC News.

Displaced Palestinians inspect the destruction following an Israeli airstrike that targeted the central Gaza Strip on Aug. 1. Majdi Fathi / NurPhoto via Getty Images

“There was not a real strategy for how long or what they should do to get to the endpoint,” the ally said.

The conflict has now entered its sixth month, despite Trump’s repeated early predictions that the war would resolve itself “shortly.”

The protracted conflict has led to soaring oil prices globally and rising gas prices in the U.S.

There was a brief reprieve from fighting in June when the U.S. and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding outlining the process for talks to end the war.

But in early July, Trump declared a ceasefire to be “over” and the countries resumed striking targets in the Middle East.

World.title: Vincent Pastore, mob enforcer on ‘The Sopranos,’ dies at 80
World.content:
Vincent Pastore, who played Tony Soprano’s best friend turned informant on HBO’s mob drama “The Sopranos,” has died, a representative confirmed Saturday.

He was 80.

Manager Robert Attermann said Pastore, a longtime resident of the Bronx borough of New York City, died at home. He confirmed that friends found his body Saturday.

A cause of death was not provided.

“To the world, he will always be remembered as the unforgettable ‘Big Pussy,’” he said, using the nickname of Pastore’s “Sopranos” character, Salvatore Bonpensiero, “but to those of us who knew him, he was so much more.”

A longtime actor who plied his trade within the sordid and violent narratives of the Italian American mob, Pastore became a household face in 1999 when he was cast cast as Bonpensiero, mob boss Tony Soprano’s best friend, a family enforcer and ultimately an FBI informant who threatened to upend the New Jersey mob’s enterprise on the acclaimed drama.

He was born in the Bronx, grew up in New Rochelle, New York, served in the U.S. Navy, and attended Pace University, according to an IMDb biography.

Vincent Pastore, left, and Tony Sirico playing cards in a scene from "The Sopranos." Anthony Neste / Getty Images

He has said he worked in the nightclub industry. But he also tried acting, and after befriending Matt Dillon and Kevin Dillon he decided to dive in, he said during a 2015 appearance on “Good Day New York.”

According to his bio at the website for HB Studio, where he was an instructor, one of Pastore’s breakthroughs as an actor was in director Nancy Savoca’s Bronx comedy “True Love.”

He also appeared on television’s “Law & Order” and as an extra in director Martin Scorsese’s 1990 mob classic “Goodfellas.” He appeared in a string of mob narratives on New York City stages and on the big screen.

Pastore became a staple in films and television dramas about organized crime, including a role in “Once Upon a Time in Brooklyn.” But it was “The Sopranos’” six-season run that made him a true star.

“His portrayal of the complex and lovable mobster earned him widespread recognition and praise,” said the Bronx Walk of Fame, which inducted the actor in 2016. “Pastore’s ability to bring depth and authenticity to his character contributed to the show’s success and solidified his place in television history.”

The character’s nickname, Big Pussy, is rumored to have originated during his time as a cat burglar. It distinguished him from another character, Little Pussy Malanga.

From left, Tony Sirico, Steven Van Zandt, James Gandolfini, Michael Imperioli and Vincent Pastore in a publicity still for "The Sopranos." Anthony Neste / Getty Images

The actor also had a musical side and performed with bands, including fronting Gangster Squad, a band familiar to small venues in New York, New Jersey and Connecticut. The band’s Facebook group says it specialized in “a mixture of classic hits from all different music genres, Rhythm and Blues, Rock & Roll, Funk, Soul, and Reggae.”

One of his most difficult gigs in the entertainment industry was during his brief 2007 stint on television’s “Dancing With the Stars,” where he lasted one week.

He said at the time that the training was too difficult.

Pastore founded Renegade Theater NYC with fellow “Sopranos” actor Maureen Van Zandt, wife of Steven Van Zandt, according to HB Studio. His Renegade Theater bio says he wrote “Crazy Horse,” describing it as “a hit play based on the story of his life as a Rock and Roll club owner.”

Musician and “Sopranos” castmate Steven Van Zandt memorialized Pastore on social media, calling him “another irreplaceable brother” who has died.

“It never gets any easier,” he said. “Travel well Vincenzo.”

Speaking on Instagram, “Sopranos” costar Michael Imperioli​ reminisced about traveling with Pastore in the United States, Italy, and Australia.

“Lots of good times,” he said. “Lots of laughs. Vinny was a kind hearted brother who cared deeply about his family and friends. I will miss him always.”

Lorraine Bracco, who played Tony Soprano’s psychiatrist on the HBO drama, said on the same platform that Pastore was “a beautiful soul.”

“Absolutely heartbreaking,” she said.

Attermann said he represented Pastore for more than 30 years — long before his HBO fame.

“Vinny was one of the kindest, most generous people I have ever known,” he said. “He treated everyone with warmth and respect, never turning down a fan who wanted a photograph or an autograph. He genuinely appreciated the people who supported him and always made them feel valued.”

Pastore “loved being an actor” and encouraging others interested in the craft, Atterman said.

He added, “I will miss his friendship, his loyalty, his humor, and his generosity. ... May his memory be a blessing.”

World.title: Truth Social launches service selling faster access to Trump posts
World.content:
Wall Street firms can now be alerted of the “most market-moving” social media posts from President Donald Trump before the general public — as long as they pay the right price.

The service went live Saturday: a subscription to his social media platform, Truth Social, that allows financial firms and other organizations to get alerts for new posts made by Trump and other top accounts before general users do.

Trump Media and Technology Group, which owns the platform, launched the new high-speed data feed called “Truth API,” describing it as giving firms “a direct, licensed, real-time feed of the platform’s most market-moving Truths.”

Trump, who has the largest following on the platform by far with 13 million followers, has used Truth Social as his go-to platform to release official statements throughout his second term, including to announce that he was imposing sweeping new tariffs or to declare major military operations.

Trump’s unprecedented use of social media to reveal updates on global affairs and economic policy has contrasted sharply with prior presidents, who generally made such announcements through more formal avenues, such as through the White House press office and the official White House website.

Many trading firms already plug into Trump’s posts through Bloomberg, Reuters or other services that scrape his posts and relay them in real time to their customers. But using this data feed on Truth Social could enable firms to access his posts seconds or even milliseconds faster than the general public.

For a high-frequency trading firm, even milliseconds could make a huge difference.

The president also stands to profit from the new service. Trump is a major stakeholder in TMTG, owning 114.75 million shares to represent 41% of the company, according to his 2025 financial disclosure.

Sens. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Adam Schiff, D-Calif., have urged the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission to investigate whether Trump Media is violating the law by selling faster access to the president’s posts.

The senators wrote that the subscription “appears to be an outrageous abuse of the President’s office for his personal benefit that undermines everyday investors and the integrity of our markets, while enriching Wall Street and other wealthy insiders.”

In its announcement of the new service last month, TMTG emphasized Truth Social’s impact on the market.

“Markets already move on Truth Social posts,” Kevin McGurn, interim chief executive officer of TMTG, said in a press release. “Truth API delivers a direct, licensed, real-time feed of the platform’s most market-moving Truths while advancing our strategy to monetize proprietary assets through a high-margin, recurring revenue stream.”

Trump launched Truth Social in early 2022 after he had been banned from X, formerly known as Twitter, and other social media platforms in 2021 following the attacks on the Capitol on Jan. 6.

Elon Musk reinstated Trump’s access to X in November 2022 shortly after he took over the platform as CEO. Trump also regained access to Facebook and Instagram in January 2023.

World.title: Trump rebukes Jeanine Pirro over decision to drop Reflecting Pool vandalism case
World.content:
President Donald Trump criticized longtime ally Jeanine Pirro Saturday after she agreed to drop a case against a former Olympic canoeist who was accused of vandalizing the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.

“I disagree 100% with Jeanine Pirro, the U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia, on the Reflecting Pool. I don’t know what she was thinking?” Trump wrote in a Truth Social post, adding “it was a pure case of VANDALISM.”

“There may have been some contractor difficulty, but the major damage was caused by VANDALS!” the president added.

Pirro’s office, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia, said Friday it had obtained information that undermined “the evidentiary basis for the indictment” against David “Davey” Hearn.

Hearn was indicted on July 2 over claims that he was “forcefully and violently pulling up and removing the bottom liner” of the pool with both hands on June 19 — shortly after the pool had undergone renovations directed by the president.

Hearn pleaded not guilty and has said that “the condition of the Reflecting Pool was the same after I stepped away from the water as it was before I got there.”

Prosecutors said Friday that they received new information from the Interior Department after Hearn’s indictment that indicated that the damage to the pool “was the result of flawed installation by the contractor, Atlantic Industrial Coatings.”

Hearn was one of several people arrested in June after the pool was seen covered in green algae and pieces of its blue sealant had peeled away in several places, resulting in chunks of the material floating on the water’s surface.

Trump, who directed a $14 million-plus renovation project that included coating the pool in “American flag blue,” has repeatedly argued that the pool’s issues were caused by vandals.

In a second post Saturday, the president argued that surveillance video clearly showed vandalism at the pool.

“Look for yourselves at the VANDALISM that took place at The Reflecting Pool. The material is being cut with a knife or a box cutter, for all to see!” Trump wrote.

On Friday, the Justice Department said it “first became aware of information showing that the damage was the result of a botched installation and not vandalism” after reviewing more documents.

The DOJ said that it wouldn’t have sought a grand jury indictment against Hearn had it initially received the documents that the Interior Department provided after the indictment.

Interior Secretary Doug Burgum continued to stand by Trump’s claims of vandalism on Saturday, despite the findings presented by Pirro’s office.

“The evidence is clear, vandals have repeatedly caused damage to the Reflecting Pool. Some of these acts were even caught on camera,” Burgum wrote in a post on X.

Burgum wrote that his office “also provided the U.S. Attorney’s office expert and eyewitness testimony to the damage done by vandals and provided every piece of evidence they asked for in the requested time line detailing each area of damage at the pool.”

Hearn’s lawyer said in a statement Friday that the Trump administration owes Hearn an apology.

“The Government’s case against Davey Hearn should never have been brought,” Steven Levin, Hearn’s attorney, said in a statement. “Its dismissal today does not erase the abuse of government power in arresting and charging a patriotic American. The government’s approach was ready, shoot, aim. The federal government owes Mr. Hearn an apology.”

Pirro’s office said Friday that it also moved to dismiss at least one of the other three misdemeanor cases against those who allegedly vandalized the pool.

World.title: Trump says he’ll revive ‘anti-weaponization’ fund if Blanche’s nomination for AG is blocked
World.content:
President Donald Trump on Saturday threatened to “push hard” to keep a $1.8 billion “anti-weaponization” fund active, amid an ongoing feud between two Republican senators and the Trump administration over the president’s nomination of Todd Blanche for attorney general.

“If Senators Cornyn and Tillis, both upset because I wouldn’t Endorse them (they lost, and quit, respectively!), aren’t going to approve Todd Blanche, one of the most respected professionals, according to everybody, in the Country, to be the United States Attorney General, then I will keep Todd as Acting A.G., and push hard to get the Anti-Weaponization Bill, which takes care of those who have been so badly treated by the Crooked Joe Biden (and Obuma!) Administration (I get nothing, although I was treated horribly!), PASSED,” the president wrote in a post on Truth Social.

“Todd Blanche was a voice of reason! It will immediately be back on the table, and I will get it done. Thank you for your attention to this matter!” he added.

Sens. John Cornyn, R-Texas, and Thom Tillis, R-N.C., are both departing Congress after feuding with Trump. In Texas, Cornyn ran for re-election, losing in a primary runoff to state Attorney General Ken Paxton after Trump endorsed Paxton.

Tillis, in North Carolina, opted not to run for re-election, making his plans to retire public one day after drawing Trump’s ire for opposing a GOP-backed domestic policy package.

The two senators have partially conditioned their support for Blanche’s nomination on the Trump administration rescinding its plans for the fund, which would provide compensation for Jan. 6 rioters pardoned by Trump for claims of government overreach.

In a post on X following Trump’s statement Saturday, Tillis blamed the president for Blanche’s stalled confirmation.

“Despite comments as late as yesterday that the fund is dead, President Trump clearly intends to resurrect the payout pot for punks either by inappropriately establishing another bogus fund or pushing Congress to vote for a bill that the majority of Republicans in the Senate would be against,” he wrote.

“It’s unfortunate that Todd Blanche, who I consider qualified for the job, will not be confirmed because of this reversal. Hopefully, we can resolve this by Tuesday,” Tillis added.

Blanche’s nomination has been in jeopardy for several weeks, with Cornyn and Tillis previously saying that there are other Republican senators that share their concerns but don’t sit on the Judiciary Committee and wouldn’t have the chance to vote for or against Blanche until his nomination came to the floor.

On Wednesday night, the committee postponed a vote on Blanche’s nomination because of Cornyn and Tillis’ concerns.

On Friday, at a Cabinet meeting, the president defended the fund, saying, “It is dead, but you know, I wish it weren’t.”

“This has nothing to do with Todd,” Trump added.

The anti-weaponization fund has been blocked indefinitely by a federal judge, but the Trump administration has not pledged to stop pursuing it.

The fund was part of a settlement agreement that stemmed from a lawsuit Trump filed against the IRS. Also part of that settlement was an agreement that made the president and several family members immune from IRS audits, another provision that Cornyn and Tillis have shared concerns about.

Earlier this week, the president threatened to withdraw Blanche’s nomination and resubmit it next year, after Tillis and Cornyn have left office.

“Hey, in 158 days they can try it again, roll the dice on what the Senate confirmation process looks like next year,” Tillis told reporters at the Capitol after that threat. “It’s all on him. Certainly within his authority to do that.”
