Además, han lanzado la botella PI de 3,14 litros, diseñada con menos material que otras alternativas equivalentes. “Permite la comodidad de una garrafa, pero es fácil de almacenar, de servir y cabe en la nevera”, describe Bravo.

Pero el objetivo de ser más responsables medioambientalmente es transversal, y empieza por el origen. “Cuidamos la diversidad del entorno del manantial”, asegura su director general. Lo hacen de la mano la Red Natura 2000, fundamental para la conservación de la naturaleza en la Unión Europea, cuyo propósito es asegurar la supervivencia a largo plazo de las especies y los tipos de hábitat. Esta red asegura la compatibilidad entre las actividades humanas y el uso adecuado del territorio.

Las fábricas de Bezoya emplean energía 100% renovable. Además, valorizan más del 90% de residuos y compensan la diferencia con reforestación, según Bravo. Toda la flota comercial es híbrida o eléctrica y las botellas están hechas en su totalidad de otras botellas recicladas.

Para trabajar en estos propósitos de forma más eficiente, en febrero la empresa matriz, Pascual, lanzó el Proyecto Aura, una reorganización que ha convertido sus distintas áreas de negocio en cinco compañías especializadas (Lácteos, Café, Distribución e Internacional, además de Hidratación). Todas mantienen un gobierno común, pero cada una cuenta ahora con un equipo propio y una hoja de ruta para adaptarse mejor a su mercado. En el caso de Bezoya, “el objetivo es trascender el agua mineral sin gas y consolidarse como una compañía centrada en la hidratación saludable”, describe Bravo, al frente de esa unidad.

Sergio Bravo, director general de Bebidas Bezoya, posa desde la embotelladora de Ortigosa del Monte (Segovia) con la Sierra de Guadarrama de fondo. Santi Burgos

Un agua de calidad

El consumidor es cada vez más exigente. “Su preocupación van más allá del precio, pide productos que no solo le ayuden a cuidar su salud, también quiere impactar lo mínimo en el medioambiente”, afirma Bravo. Por eso, responden con “máxima coherencia” y con mineralización muy débil (’Para vivir muy fuerte’, dice su lema). Como apunta Pardo, esta tipología “puede generar en el organismo una especie de limpieza. Las células del torrente sanguíneo están cargadas con distintos minerales y, al tener el agua una mineralización muy baja, si esa concentración es alta, la arrastra”. En cambio, si el agua tiene una mineralización media, el equilibrio se mantiene y, si es alta, aporta más electrolitos y minerales, “lo que ayuda a recuperar las sales”.

Pardo, como responsable de Calidad, se asegura de que el producto llegue al consumidor con las mismas propiedades con las que emerge del manantial. “El agua viene así de la montaña: es buena y pura, con una composición estable químicamente”, explica. La travesía hasta que llega al envase da comienzo en la sierra de Guadarrama, en un perímetro de protección al que llaman la zona de captación. Allí, la pluviometría (la lluvia o la precipitación que cae) se filtra por un terreno granítico, un tipo de suelo que deja esa mineralización tan baja.

Carla Pardo, la responsable de Calidad de las plantas de Bezoya, en el laboratorio de Ortigosa del Monte (Segovia). SANTI BURGOS

El alumbramiento, la primera vez que se ve el agua, es ya dentro de la botella. Después pasa por el etiquetado, el loteado y el empaquetado, y ya queda lista para que el consumidor la beba. En todo momento, su temperatura se mantiene fría. “En invierno es aproximadamente de 9 grados y en verano puede llegar hasta los 13″, indica la experta.

En la zona de captación “no hay absolutamente nada; ni pozos ni ninguna extracción externa, porque el agua nos llega por gravedad”, describe la segoviana. Tampoco realizan intervenciones en el entorno más allá de la construcción necesaria para la planta que, en los últimos años, se ha ampliado. Sergio Moreno ha sido testigo de esta evolución: “Me motiva haber llegado desde abajo y ser parte de estos cambios; la fábrica, la línea, la formatos... Todo se ha modernizado”. Una evolución que, más allá de la adaptación a las demandas de los clientes y a la sostenibilidad, permite que el trabajo perdure, los puestos se mantengan y la comarca logre una población estable.

A Moreno el trabajo en cadena le gusta; le permite ayudar al compañero que va antes y al que va después. “He podido coordinar equipos y conocerles de primera mano. Algunas veces ayudo a personas que ya estaban cuando entré, y noto cómo he crecido. Es muy bonito”, confiesa. También se enorgullece del resultado, del producto final: “Vas de vacaciones y ves botellas de Bezoya. Además, a la gente le encanta. Es muy gratificante”, resume.

World.title: De amores y afinidades entre los escritores y los gatos
World.content:
Artículos estrictamente de opinión que responden al estilo propio del autor. Estos textos de opinión han de basarse en datos verificados y ser respetuosos con las personas aunque se critiquen sus actos. Todas las columnas de opinión de personas ajenas a la Redacción de EL PAÍS llevarán, tras la última línea, un pie de autor —por conocido que éste sea— donde se indique el cargo, título, militancia política (en su caso) u ocupación principal, o la que esté o estuvo relacionada con el tema abordado

Siempre ha habido secretas simpatías entre los gatos, la soledad, los libros y el silencio. Los príncipes de este mundo se han hecho retratar con perros y caballos, mientras que el gato quedó para posar en el regazo bien acolchado de los cardenales. Es animal de interior, y todavía hoy una biblioteca será más biblioteca si un gato se pasea por entre los lomos de los libros con indiferencia de dama de bolero. Según Von Betchen, “el gato se parece a lo que los escritores querrían ser”: es decir, gentes independientes y caracteres sin sobresaltos. Y aún podríamos añadir: tanto a los escritores como a los gatos les gusta el mismo tipo de vida, sofá orejero por el día; escapada y aventura al caer la noche.

Cuando un petimetre de Oxford le pidió consejo para iniciar su carrera literaria, Aldous Huxley no lo dudó: “Si usted quiere escribir, tenga gatos”. En el sur de Europa el gato es animal tiñoso de exteriores, y en España las clases pijas han aborrecido a los gatos, a saber si por preferir los toros. En otros países civilizados y lluviosos el gato era, sin embargo, un animal tan ornamental como su reproducción en porcelana. Gatófilo ejemplar, Paul Léautaud decía ser el escritor más libre de Francia por ser también el más pobre. En su casa llegó a acumular más de 300 gatos, recogidos aquí y allá por los arrabales de París. Los escritores han sido, en todo caso, siempre proyectivos y pretenciosos con los nombres: Colette llamó a una gata Kiki-la-Doucette y tuvo el acierto de llamar a otro Prr. Lilith se llamaba la gata de Mallarmé, lo que sin duda le pega a Mallarmé, y uno no sabe en qué pensaba el viejo Anatole France al imponer a su gato nada menos que el nombre de Amílcar, que es como llamar Gandhi a un rottweiler. Nunca hemos sabido el nombre del gato de Dante, pero del de Petrarca se sabe que el poeta le escribió un epitafio.

Pla dejó escrito cuanto hay de esfíngico en los gatos al afirmar que “todo en el gato es dogma, seriedad y forma eterna”. Como animal escrito, el gato tiene una prosapia de gran tono. Teófilo Gautier, Colette y Kipling le dedicaron novelitas, y Eliot les dedicó un libro de poemas. En todo caso, su vate de más fama será para siempre Baudelaire, que no tuvo el menor problema a la hora de rimar “magiques” con “mystiques” en su alabanza. Neruda lo llamó “mínimo tigre de salón” y ya no sé quién dijo aquello de que Dios había creado al gato para que pudiésemos acariciar a un tigre. Y, de gato escrito a gato pintado, una iconografía para aplaudir: el gato que captura ratones como imagen de Cristo en busca de las almas.

La política nos ha dejado felinos de interés como Larry, el ratonero de Downing Street, que va ya por su sexto primer ministro en Downing Street, con el pienso garantizado por el presupuesto público. Con todo, y sin salir de Londres, el gato más conocido de la historia también ha tenido más que ver con las letras que con las armas. Del gato Hodge sabemos lo que nos cuenta James Boswell: que el doctor Johnson se aliviaba sus melancolías de erudito, tan intensas, jugando con él, y que se ocupaba personalmente de comprarle la comida, no fuera que los sirvientes —decía el prohombre— le cogieran rabia a “la pobre criatura” si tenían que ir de mandados ellos. Viejo y sabio, el doctor Johnson conocía la impiedad de sus hermanos los hombres con lo que es más desnudo e indefenso.

Cuando Hodge ya estaba en la ronda de la muerte, el gran lexicógrafo tuvo que cumplir con un deber de piedad: comprarle la valeriana para aliviar su tránsito. Y cabe imaginar que aquel recado le resultaría penoso, toda vez que Boswell, que abominaba de los gatos, nos relata cómo Johnson dejaba que Hodge se paseara por su pecho, mientras el escritor “sonreía y silbaba entre dientes”, un solaz que no era sino un paréntesis de alegría pura de vivir, de afecto y desenfado para un sabio de carácter en ocasiones funéreo. Y no sé si Johnson era un animalista o si tan sólo sabía que la mirada de los animales nos devuelve nuestra propia humanidad, y que por eso hay que tratarlos con el respeto que merece toda la naturaleza que pena y sufre y muere, más aún cuando “la pobre criatura” le había dado tan gratuitamente ocasión de sonreír. Hoy a Hodge le honran una estatua en Londres, una cita al comienzo del Pálido fuego de Nabokov, y hasta nosotros, querido lector, que hemos engañado nuestras melancolías evocándolo.

World.title: ‘Ted Lasso’ en Apple TV, ‘The Shards’ en Disney+ y otras series recomendadas para agosto
World.content:
Este será uno de los meses más flojos en cuestión de series de los últimos años. Agosto siempre ha sido un mes de transición, a medio camino entre los títulos pensados para el verano, que se estrenan hacia junio y julio, y las novedades de la temporada otoñal, que aguardan su turno en septiembre y octubre. El entrenador de fútbol más famoso de la ficción televisiva, Ted Lasso, regresa este mes con una cuarta temporada. También este mes se completará la historia de Macondo en formato serie. Y los superhéroes Green Lanterns cobran vida con Damon Lindelof a los mandos de la adaptación.

Además, la serie de acción con Zoe Saldaña y Nicole Kidman Lioness regresa con una tercera temporada (día 3 en SkyShowtime). Las aventuras espaciales de Futurama siguen expandiéndose con su 14ª entrega (día 4 en Disney+). Sterling Point (día 5 en Prime Video) sigue a dos adolescentes que se mudan con su padre adoptivo a la isla que acaban de heredar. Otra propuesta con enfoque juvenil es Mi vida con los chicos Walter, que regresa con su tercera temporada (día 6 en Netflix). Y otra más es Outer Banks (día 20 en Netflix), que ya llega a su quinta y última temporada.

La comedia española Muertos S.L. termina su recorrido con su cuarta entrega (día 7 en Netflix). Reacher (día 12 en Prime Video) continúa las andanzas de este policía militar retirado. El thriller británico Dos semanas de agosto (día 13 en Movistar Plus) lleva a sus protagonistas a Grecia. La segunda temporada de Los Hardacre (día 20 en Movistar Plus) continúa la historia de una familia de nuevos ricos. Y el thriller de ciencia ficción Materia oscura regresa con su segunda temporada (día 28 en Apple TV).

De los estrenos y regresos de este mes (que puede consultar en nuestro calendario), recomendamos dar una oportunidad a esta selección.

Cien años de soledad

02:19 Tráiler de la segunda temporada de 'Cien años de soledad' Una imagen de la segunda temporada de 'Cien años de soledad'.

La traslación a la pantalla de la obra magna de Gabriel García Márquez concluirá este mes en Netflix con su segunda y última temporada. Los nuevos episodios retoman la historia tras la muerte de José Arcadio Buendía y la firma del armisticio en Macondo. De todas formas, la paz no llegará a la ciudad. La llegada de Fernanda del Campo dará un giro en la familia y el tranvía abrirá las puertas de Macondo a la compañía bananera, lo que derivará en una tragedia. La segunda parte de la serie se aleja del realismo mágico para acercarse más al contexto político, histórico y social en el que se desarrolla y que llevará al esplendor y la caída de Macondo

¿Cuándo y dónde verla? El miércoles 5 se estrenan siete episodios, y el octavo y último llegará el miércoles 26 de agosto.

Ted Lasso

Jason Sudeikis y Hannah Waddingham, en el primer capítulo de la cuarta temporada de 'Ted Lasso'. Apple TV

Parecía haber terminado, pero no. La historia de ese entrenador de fútbol americano que es contratado por un equipo de la Premier League inglesa y termina ganándose el corazón de jugadores y aficionados parecía que había cerrado con su tercera temporada. Pero Apple TV tenía en esta comedia amable a uno de sus mayores éxitos y no la podía dejar escapar así como así, y tres años después, aquí está de vuelta. Tras marcharse a Kansas, Ted recibirá una oferta de sus antiguos compañeros para regresar a Richmond y hacerse cargo del equipo femenino, donde tendrá que volver a desplegar sus escasos conocimientos futbolísticos y sus habilidades sociales y su empatía para hacerse con las riendas. Sus espectadores ya saben lo que se encontrarán: más sonrisas que carcajadas y personajes que llevan la amabilidad por bandera (incluso cuando gruñen tanto como Roy Kent).

¿Cuándo y dónde verla? El miércoles 5 se estrena el primer episodio en Apple TV y seguirán capítulos semanales hasta el 7 de octubre.

The Shards

01:55 Tráiler de la serie 'The Shards' Los protagonistas de la serie 'The Shards'.

El mundo de privilegio en el que vive el joven Bret, aspirante a escritor a punto de comenzar su último año de instituto, y sus compañeros se tambalea cuando en su entorno empiezan a desaparecer jóvenes y tienen lugar unos macabros asesinatos rituales. Al mismo tiempo, se incorpora a clase un nuevo compañero con muchos secretos. En realidad, todos ellos tienen secretos. El prolífico guionista y productor Ryan Murphy se alía en este caso con el escritor Bret Easton Ellis para adaptar la novela semiautobiográfica de este último ambientada en los círculos más elitistas de Los Ángeles en los años ochenta. Un thriller con aire ochentero que combina temas como la identidad sexual, el autodescubrimiento o la obsesión.

¿Cuándo y dónde verla? Disney+ estrena los dos primeros episodios el jueves 6.

Linternas

02:53 Tráiler de la serie 'Linternas' Aaron Pierre y Kyle Chandler, protagonistas de la serie 'Linternas'.

Esta serie del universo DC tiene varios elementos que nos hace prestar especial atención. Por un lado, detrás de ella está Damon Lindelof (Perdidos, The Leftovers, Watchmen), cocreador de la serie junto al autor del cómic, Tom King, y el guionista y productor Chris Mundy, que ejerce como showrunner. El tono parece que estará más cerca del noir que de las habituales historias de superhéroes, a juzgar por el tráiler. La historia sigue a dos policías intergalácticos, uno veterano, interpretado por Kyle Chandler, y un joven recluta, al que da vida Aaron Pierre. Sus investigaciones en la Tierra les llevará a verse envueltos en un oscuro misterio y enfrentarse a un peligro para los humanos.

¿Cuándo y dónde verla? El primero de sus ocho episodios se estrena el lunes 17 en HBO Max.

El patíbulo

00:43 Tráiler en inglés de la serie 'El patíbulo' Sophie McShera y Michael Socha, en la serie 'El patíbulo'.

El director Shane Meadows (This Is England, The Virtues) es el responsable de esta serie británica de 2023 que en su momento recibió aplausos y que permanecía inédita en España. La historia, que adapta una novela de Benjamin Myers y se basa en hechos reales, sigue a una banda de falsificadores en el Yorkshire del siglo XVIII. La Revolución Industrial y la pujanza de Halifax como centro del comercio de la zona provocó el empobrecimiento de pueblos que antes habían sido foco de una próspera industria textil. Para tratar de salir del pozo, un hombre reclutará a otros vecinos, tejedores y trabajadores de la tierra, para poner en marcha una estafa de monedas que derivará en el mayor fraude en la historia británica.

¿Cuándo y dónde verla? La serie de tres episodios se estrena el martes 18 en Filmin.

Toda la verdad de mis mentiras

02:04 Tráiler de la serie 'Toda la verdad de mis mentiras'. Itziar Manero, Lucía de la Fuente, Clara Sans y Brays Efe, en el primer capítulo de 'Toda la verdad de mis mentiras'.

La cuarta adaptación que Netflix hace de una historia escrita por Elísabet Benavent sigue a un grupo de amigos en un viaje en autocaravana en la despedida de soltera de una de ellas. La protagonista de la historia, Coco, lleva años compartiendo piso con Marín y son mejores amigos. Pero empieza a notar que quizá sus sentimientos reales vayan más allá. No será la única que oculte secretos dentro del grupo que se da cita en este road trip. Itziar Manero, Daniel Ibáñez, Lucía de la Fuente, Clara Sans, Ricardo Gómez y Brays Efe son los protagonistas de estos cinco episodios sobre la amistad, relaciones cruzadas y las mentiras con las que nos engañamos a nosotros mismos.

¿Cuándo y dónde verla? En Netflix, el viernes 28 de agosto.

World.title: “Amsterdam’s gay tourism scene doesn’t stretch beyond the city”
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

For over two decades, Michiel Hoogkamer has single-handedly managed Leiden’s sole gay bar. As it approaches its final weeks in business, he and others speak to Brandon Hartley about the challenges facing the country’s ‘homohoreca’ [gay nightlife scene].

Michiel Hoogkamer, the owner of De Roze Beurs, Leiden’s only gay bar, is ready

to call it quits.

After 24 years of catering for everyone from introverted university students to boisterous drag queens, the final night has been set for 15 August.

There’s no single reason why Hoogkamer decided to close down the bar he lovingly described as his child during an interview with Dutch News, but it comes at a difficult time for LGBTI+ oriented businesses all across the Netherlands.

While De Roze Beurs continues to host a stream of regulars, similar businesses across the country have struggled over the past decade.

“Here in the Netherlands, little bars like this one aren’t doing well,” Hoogkamer said. “Young people aren’t loyal to one place anymore. They go to monthly or quarterly parties at nightclubs instead or go to restaurants in the middle of the day.”

Hoogkamer and others say the country’s homohoreca is facing an increasing number of challenges.

Homohoreca is a Dutch term for hospitality businesses that cater for a gay, lesbian, transgender, and bisexual clientele, such as bars, saunas, nightclubs, and restaurants.

Saunas disappearing

Even Amsterdam is not immune. Cafe Getto, a popular gay-oriented restaurant that became famous for its ‘Diva Burgers,’ closed down a few years ago.

Lola the Green Aardvark, a queer food bar, and the lesbian/bisexual/queer café B’Femme both shuttered in 2025.

“The decline is drastic among gay saunas,” Peter Koop told Dutch News. “In 2020, there were still 12 gay saunas, but only eight remain.

“The closed saunas have not found successors. This is likely because there is hardly any interest in such establishments among young people anymore.”

Koop is the current writer and editor of homohoreca.nl, a website that has been tracking the industry since 2001.

However, a precise forecast of what’s to come could prove more difficult than predicting the weather in April.

“Although we do not have hard figures, we also have the impression that there are fewer bars and clubs aimed at the LGBTI+ community,” Philip Tijsma, spokesperson for the national LGBTQ+ rights group COC Nederland, said.

Changing habits

Many clientele are less reliant on these businesses to serve as safe spaces or

dating venues.

“We also have the impression that people’s nightlife behaviour has changed,’ Tijsma said.

“People go to a bar or club less often, and are more likely to attend a large LGBTI+ party or festival a few times a year. General nightlife venues have also sometimes become more inclusive and LGBTI+ people feel at home there more often.”

“In the Netherlands, there is indeed a decline in the number of gay bars, but that decline is very slow,” Koop said.

He said an average of two close in the Netherlands every year, but at least one new one usually appears.

Gay tourism

Koop also noted that, despite a downturn between 2010 and 2015, the number in Amsterdam has been holding steady.

“Amsterdam’s gay establishments benefit from gay tourism, which is not the case in the rest of the Netherlands,” he said.

The decrease is less severe than many people think, but the blow can be hard locally, as is the case with Leiden.”

The city still has a local chapter of COC Nederland but, aside from periodic club nights, it’s more of an advocacy centre than a social organisation.

Potential buyers

The building that houses De Roze Beurs has primarily served as a bar since it was built in 1636.

The name is somewhat difficult to translate into English, as beurs can mean various things such as stock exchange, marketplace and coin purse.

Hoogkamer said the name is partially a tribute to the years it was used as a meeting hall for officials and accountants from the Beestenmarkt, a nearby square where livestock was once sold.

He doesn’t know what the future holds for the building, but he doubts it will remain a gay bar.

A few interested parties have approached him about taking over De Roze Beurs, but the discussions didn’t go far. His landlord will make the ultimate decision about what happens next.

Homophobia increasing

Additional challenges new owners might face include what Hoogkamer says has been a rise in anti-gay hostility.

He said his first few years behind the bar could be rough at times. At one point in the early 2000s, the building was attacked by someone who threw paint bombs at the windows.

Things were largely quiet throughout the 2010s, but there’s been an uptick in aggression after De Roze Beurs reopened following the pandemic.

The rainbow flags out front have been stolen several times. On a busy Saturday night, a vandal smashed one of the windows and shouted anti-gay slurs at his customers.

Berlin attack

Hoogkamer also says there’s been an increase in passers-by heckling patrons seated outside on the terrace.

Recent studies suggest gay tolerance has declined in the Netherlands, especially among youths.

The Berlin Pride attack paints an even darker picture of the situation elsewhere

around the world.

“With the extreme right coming up, like Wilders and the FvD, it’s getting worse,” Hoogkamer said.

“They all say they’re woke and they’re attracting a lot of young people, but it simply isn’t true.”

Late nights

There’s also no denying that running any sort of bar can be incredibly difficult, especially once you enter middle age.

De Roze Beurs is essentially a one-man operation. “It’s hard work and I sometimes have 80-hour working weeks,” Hoogkamer said. “As you get older, you start to feel it, and there’s the long nights.

“I don’t get to bed until four or five in the morning. Everybody else gets to go home and I have to stay here and clean the toilets.”

When Dutch News recently visited De Roze Beurs, many of the rubber ducks that once stood watch over the bar itself had been packed up and placed into bags with other memorabilia.

Stripper pole

Along with an iconic stripper pole and pretty much everything else, the ducks will be sold at an auction scheduled for 20 August hosted by local drag queen Christine Carrington.

Hoogkamer will be sad to see it all go, but he said he was ready to move on.

“I’m going on sabbatical for a year,” he said. “I’m 46, I have good legs, and I want to see something of the world after managing a bar for so many years.”

While he himself wouldn’t take over a gay bar nowadays, he said Leiden could still use one, especially if there’s a person out there who knows what they’re getting themselves into.

“There’s plenty of potential in this city for a gay or queer bar, but you have to work hard,” he advised. “You’re not going to get rich and your social life is forever on hold.

“You can’t go to parties and you can’t go to birthdays because they’re all on Fridays and Saturdays. When do you make your money? On Fridays and Saturdays.”

World.title: Dutch unions call 24-hour public transport strike on September 9
World.content:
Public transport workers across the Netherlands are to stage a one-day strike on Wednesday, September 9, bringing buses, trains, trams and metro services almost to a standstill.

The FNV union has called the strike in the latest escalation of its campaign against the government’s social welfare reforms, which it says will lead to lower living standards for millions of working people.

The three major unions FNV, CNV and VCP have vowed to fight the cabinet’s social welfare reforms, which are designed to secure €6.5 billion in cost savings during the goverment’s four-year term.

Social affairs minister Hans Vijlbrief scrapped a plan to increase the statutory retirement age faster by raising it in step with life expectancy, but the unions want the cabinet to go further by abandoning cuts to unemployment pay and long-term disability benefits.

Staff working for NS, ProRail, urban and regional transport sevices and DB cargo will down tools for 24 hours on September 9, making it impossible to run timetables.

Delays inevitable

“We are aware that a 24-hour strike will cause disruption,” said FNV official Edwim Kuiper. “We regret that deeply. But the consequences of the dismantling of our social security are much greater for everyone and will last much longer.”

National train operator NS said it could not say exactly what the impact of the stoppage would be because it had not been officially notified by the union.

Lobby organisation OV-NL, which represents nine smaller public transport companies such as Arriva, QBuzz and the major city network operators GVB, RET and HTM, said it “understood up to a point” the reason to call a strike.

But it said it was “very unfortunate that passengers are being disadvantaged by a social and political debate”.

Union leader Henri Janssen said that the strike was being called on behalf of commuters. “Every working person has to deal with sickness, work incapacity or involuntary unemployment. They should be able to count on a decent social safety net,“ he said.

World.title: Amsterdam steps up Pride security in wake of attack in Berlin
World.content:
Amsterdam has stepped up security around this weekend’s WorldPride street parties and the annual canal parade in the wake of last week’s attack in Berlin.

A total of 250 concrete blocks have been placed along the canals and nightclubs are carrying out extra bag searches during the two-week event, which runs until August 8.

Richard Keldoulis of Club Church, one of Amsterdam’s best known gay clubs, told NOS: “I’ve never known anything like this.”

Venue owners are in constant contact with the police and intelligence services about appropriate security measures, although they conceded that it is almost impossible to prevent a so-called “lone wolf” attack by one person using a knife or a vehicle.

Last Sunday a woman was killed and 29 people were injured when a man drove a car into a crowd near the Brandenburg Gate in Berlin, where the annual Christopher Street Day parade, Germany’s main Pride event, was taking place.

The suspect, Abdul B., was later shot dead by police, who have said they are treating the incident as an Islamist terrorist attack.

Lone wolf attacks

“I come from Berlin and I was at the scene of the attack last week. I left the party few minutes before it all went wrong, but my friends were still there,” Keldoulis said.

“It’s always nice to feel safe, but ultimately you can never rule it out altogether. There were barriers and security measures in Berlin as well, but it still went wrong.”

Michel Peters, chair of the gay police association Roze in Blauw (“pink in blue”), said police would maintain a high-visibility presence during the weekend.

“We are there mainly to maintain contact with the [LGBTQI+] community,” he said. “We want to do more to show that we are there in the coming dys, so that people know they can approach us when something is going on.”

On Tuesday evening thousands of people in Amsterdam gathered at the Homomonument, the national memorial to victims of homophobic persecution, to commemorate the victims of Berlin.

City mayor Femke Halsema addressed the crowd, calling for courage and resilience. “We will win if we keep spreading hope loud and clear,” she said.

World.title: Dutch inflation rises to 3.1% in July as fuel costs soar
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Inflation rose slightly to 3.1% in July, sustaining the above-target trend of the last two and a half years, according to statistics agency CBS’s latest flash forecast.

A 9.7% spike in energy prices, including motor fuels, was the main driver of the increase as overall inflation ticked up from 2.9% in June.

Services inflation was measured at 4.1%, the same level as in June, while purchases abroad were 4.8% more expensive, down from 5.7% a month ago.

The harmonised European rate, which does not include the costs associated with owning or renting a home, was measured at 2.9%, up from 2.5% in June.

Since January 2024 inflation in the Netherlands has been persistently above the European Central Bank’s target level of 2%, peaking at 4.1% in December 2024 and April 2025. Its highest level so far this year was 3.5% in May.

The Dutch government has so far resisted calls to cut prices at the pumps, even though the Netherlands has the most expensive fuel in Europe, at €2.35 for a litre of petrol and €2.39 for diesel.

The CBS will publish the confirmed results with a more detailed breakdown on August 11.

World.title: Woman finds dinner-plate sized tarantula in her garden
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

A woman in Twente was enjoying the sunshine in her garden on Wednesday when she came face to face with a tarantula the size of a dinner plate.

Dierenambulance Enschede posted photos of the poisonous spider on social media after they were called to the town of Oldenzaal to retrieve the arachnid.

The woman spotted the creature in her yard and informed the regional animal ambulance, who were able to capture it by placing a container over the creature and slowly sliding the lid underneath.

Tarantulas do not live in the wild in the Netherlands and it is suspected the spider escaped from a neighbour’s house.

According to the Dierenambulance Enschede, tarantulas are largely harmless. Their bites are akin to a wasp sting.

A number of people admitted they would not have had the woman’s composure. “If I had found the spider, this spider would now be the new owner of my former house,” one commenter wrote on the animal organisation Facebook post.

World.title: Arne Slot rules himself out as next Netherlands head coach
World.content:
Former Liverpool and Feyenoord coach Arne Slot has ruled himself out as the next manager of the Dutch men’s national team, saying he wants to keep working in club football.

The 47-year-old was one of the names put forward to succeed Ronald Koeman, who resigned after the Netherlands were knocked out of the World Cup by Morocco in the round of 32.

Slot has also been courted by AC Milan and English Premier League side Fulham since he was sacked by Liverpool at the end of May after two seasons in charge.

The Dutchman, who arrived after steering Feyenoord to only their second Eredivisie title since the turn of the century, won the Premier League in his first season but could only manage fifth place last term.

The Dutch football association KNVB wants to appoint a manager well ahead of the next UEFA Nations League match against Germany on September 24.

Two other potential successors have also dropped out of the running. PSV manager Peter Bosz has extended his contract at the Eindhoven club, while former Ajax head coach Erik ten Hag recently joined his home town club Twente Enschede as director of football and has said he wants to continue in that role.

World.title: “I will always want to have a home in Amsterdam”
World.content:
Originally from the Philippines, Deepa Paul moved to Amsterdam nearly 15 years ago after her husband took a job in the capital. Her book about opening up her marriage, Ask Me How It Works, was longlisted for the Women’s Prize for Non-Fiction. She loves how the Dutch do kids birthday parties, strongly advises tourists not to cycle and wishes she could have met Mata Hari.

How did you end up in the Netherlands?

I was born in the Philippines to a Bengali father and Filipina mother. I met my husband at university in Manila. I was studying communication but also had a crazy pipe dream of going to Europe to train as a classical singer. His first job ended up being in Singapore, so we had a long-distance relationship for four years while I lived in Manila. After we were married, I moved to Singapore to be with him and found work as a writer and producer in TV. But Singapore wasn’t really my bag.

I pitched my husband the idea of one last adventure before having a baby: a round-the-world trip, him on unpaid sabbatical, me writing freelance. He thought I was crazy and suggested finding a job abroad instead.

A friend working at a Dutch multinational offered to put him in touch with a VP at their Amsterdam HQ. I remember thinking that the cold email my husband wrote sounded way too direct and maybe a bit too much. Turns out the Dutch are a direct culture: it worked! One job offer and six months later, we were on a one-way flight to Amsterdam.

How do you describe yourself – an expat, lovepat, immigrant, international?

I am an immigrant.

How long do you plan to stay?

I don’t see an end date. I will always want to have a home in Amsterdam, although I often fantasise about living a parallel existence somewhere warm in the winter.

Do you speak Dutch and how did you learn?

There’s nothing glamorous about how I accumulated the Dutch I speak now, which I’d describe as pretty passable for daily social life. It was one awkward conversation with one school parent at a time, lots of listening to how people actually talk, and relying on context clues to fill in the 20-30% I might not be grasping accurately when people talk fast.

My husband had negotiated 30 hours of Dutch lessons for both of us, through his employer, when he started his job. I paused for a year or two after I gave birth to my daughter, then went back and took classes at the Volksuniversiteit.

I find that when Dutch people switch to English with me, I can push back. My go-to phrase is ‘ik ben grappiger in het Engels’ [I’m funnier in English]. Humour is disarming, it smooths over the switch in social situations..

My greatest achievement was being interviewed live on NPO Radio 1 about my book in Dutch. The segment was only supposed to last 8 minutes, but it was the longest 11 minutes of my life! Turns out talking about love, commitment, sex and open marriage is far more complicated than chatting about the weather.

What’s your favourite Dutch thing?

You’re asking a polyamorist to choose just one?! I love the mobility and freedom of cycling. Gezelligheid. The simplicity of young children’s birthday parties. The straightforward ease of voting — if you don’t come from a culture of systemically corrupt and murderous elections, as I do, you might not appreciate what a privilege and relief that is. The progression of flowers in the spring, from tulips to hyacinths to cherry blossoms to peonies to roses to dahlias: what a gift it is to have a reliable abundance of beauty.

How Dutch have you become?

Not much — I’m still too short (1.56m). I would argue that living in the Netherlands has given me the space and independence to become more myself, rather than more Dutch.

Having said that, I am a lot more direct now, and I not only can handle direct communication, I prefer it. It’s quite a relief actually, coming from a conflict-avoidant, high-context culture. I’ve been nearly cured of my lifelong affliction of Filipino time, which means I’m only mildly late most of the time, and actually punctual the rest of the time.

Which three Dutch people (dead or alive) would you most like to meet?

Anne Frank, who inspired me to start keeping a journal at the age of nine. She was the first person to show me that writing about my inner world and observing my own life, no matter how small and ordinary, is a worthy endeavour.

Rachel Ruysch, the most prolific and commercially successful female artist of the Dutch Golden Age, whose floral still life paintings sold for more than Rembrandt’s paintings in that time.

Mata Hari, born Margaretha Geertruida Zelle in Friesland, a bold free spirit who harnessed her eroticism, feminine power and artistic expression to live a courageous life and extraordinary life for a woman of her time. Later biographies exonerated her of espionage in World War I, but her image as a powerful and mysterious femme fatale endures to this day.

What’s your top tourist tip?

Please don’t cycle in Amsterdam, especially not with your selfie stick out. It’s not Disneyland with tulips and windmills along every cycle path. Some of us have things to do and places to get to.

On a less grumpy note, try to book a visit to the Six Collection in advance. It’s a private art collection that spans over three centuries and 10 generations of the wealthy and influential Six family, who have one of the most celebrated Rembrandt paintings you’ve never seen hanging right in their living room.

Tell us something surprising you’ve found out about the Netherlands.

When I gave birth in 2013, I was taken aback that official paternity leave was two days — one day for the actual birth and a second day for the father to register it. It ran completely counter to the image of the Netherlands in my mind as egalitarian, progressive and liberal. It turns out that it’s still deeply patriarchal in small, hidden and entrenched ways.

If you had just 24 hours left in the Netherlands, what would you do?

If I’m not panicking about making sure everything is packed and ready to go, cycle around my neighbourhood and have a coffee at my favourite spots. If the weather allows, go for a walk and read in the sunshine at Westerpark, then go for a dip in the IJ.

Throw a big party at home for all the friends I’ve made over the last 15 years, all the people who have become part of my story (except those I’ve revoked access to). My husband will cook enough Filipino food to feed everyone one last time. Eat, drink, laugh, cry, hug and dance, maybe stay up talking until the sun comes up.

If we make it out early enough, go dancing until my legs give out or the club kicks us out. Cycle home as the sun rises and enjoy one last sleep in my own bed—or not.

Deepa was speaking to Molly Quell.

Dutch drug criminal Jos Leijdekkers, known as Bolle Jos, has been convicted by a Belgian judge and sentenced to 14 years in prison.

The 35-year old was not present at the court in Antwerp when the verdict was announced on Thursday, having been on the run since 2024.

Leijdekkers was sentenced for his part in the Costa drugs case, in which a total of 56 people were accused of smuggling 25 tonnes of cocaine through Antwerp and money laundering. The drugs had a street value of €3.5 billion.

An investigation by Follow The Money revealed that the Brabant drugs baron has been living in Sierre Leone and is in a relationship with the president’s daughter.

Two years ago, a Dutch judge sentenced him to 24 years in 2024 for cocaine trafficking through the ports of Antwerp and Rotterdam.

In total, he has been sentenced to 103 years in prison across 10 trials.

The Dutch have requested his extradition from Sierre Leone, but the government denies any knowledge of his presence in the country.

According to drugs experts, the West African country has become a major logistical hub for the smuggling of drugs from South America to Europe.

Earlier this year, Spanish authorities intercepted a ship that had departed from the country and discovered 30,215 kilograms of cocaine, the largest intercepted cocaine shipment ever.

A Canadian multinational operator of convenience stores, Alimentation Couche-Tard, has announced plans to acquire Poland’s Żabka Group, which runs Europe’s largest chain of convenience stores. The company has offered 32 zloty per share, valuing Żabka at 32.6 billion zloty (€7.56 billion). Żabka’s main shareholders have agreed to sell their stakes, with final approval still required from stock market investors. If the transaction is completed, Żabka is likely to be delisted from the Warsaw Stock Exchange just two years after its market debut. Właściciel Circle K chce przejąć 100% Żabki. Alimentation Couche-Tard has already secured commitments to acquire at least 57.2% of the company. Heket, an entity linked to CVC Capital Partners owning 37.6% of Żabka’s shares, and PG Investment Company, holding 10%, have agreed to sell their entire stakes. A group of major individual shareholders, together controlling 9.6% of Żabka’s shares, has also agreed to sell its holdings to the Canadian buyer. The investors include members of the company’s management and former executives. They have also agreed to reinvest part of the proceeds from the sale into Alimentation Couche-Tard shares. The tender offer for the remaining shares was announced on Friday by Ipopema Securities, which is acting as the intermediary in the transaction. Alimentation Couche-Tard and Żabka expect subscriptions for the offer to open around 26 August, following a review of the tender document by the Polish Financial Supervision Authority (KNF). The companies foresee the transaction closing by the end of the year. The Canadian company expects Żabka to continue operating independently, under the leadership of its current management team, and to retain its brand. Żabka shares jumped after the announcement, rising from 29.26 zloty to around 31.60 zloty on Friday afternoon, an increase of about 8%. World.title: The split in Poland’s opposition could help them unseat Tusk’s government [Opinion]
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. By Daniel Tilles If Mateusz Morawiecki cuts his final ties with PiS and forms a new party, it may help broaden the opposition’s appeal by offering voters a more moderate, centre-right option. While the strings have not yet been fully cut, Poland’s main opposition party, the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), is splitting in two. A group of 40 MPs led by former Prime Minister (and PiS deputy leader) Mateusz Morawiecki have now formed a separate parliamentary caucus of their own, after last week refusing to sign a pledge of loyalty and quit the association they had formed – as had been demanded by PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński. Former Polish PM @MorawieckiM says 41 lawmakers aligned with him will form their own parliamentary caucus, deepening a split in conservative opposition party @pisorgpl. The proposed group would become the third-largest bloc in Poland's Sejmhttps://t.co/coOdpS7pia — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 29, 2026 The move means that Morawiecki’s caucus, known as Development Plus (Rozwój Plus), is now the third largest in parliament, while PiS, which is down to 147 MPs, has lost its status as the biggest. For now, most of Morawiecki’s followers officially remain members of the PiS party, a situation that will only change if they either resign or are thrown out following a disciplinary process that could take weeks. But unless either or both sides make major concessions, it seems only a matter of time before Development Plus becomes a separate party. A lot of international reporting has suggested that these developments will harm Poland’s right-wing opposition and boost the re-election chances of Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s more liberal coalition at next year’s parliamentary elections. In fact, PiS’s split could well help the opposition win a majority. Over the last year, PiS has found itself in an increasingly difficult position. Its support in the polls has fallen below 25%, the party’s lowest level in 14 years. Meanwhile, combined support for two far-right opposition groups – Confederation (Konfederacja) and Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP) – has risen to over 20%, threatening PiS’s longstanding dominance on the right. In response, Kaczyński has pushed his party in a more rightward direction, picking a hardline figure, Przemysław Czarnek, as PiS’s prime ministerial candidate in March. That signalled that PiS was aiming to compete head to head with the far right on many issues, taking tougher positions on Ukraine, the EU, migration and climate policy. In many cases, that meant disowning the legacy of the PiS government led by Morawiecki from 2017 to 2023. It also meant that the party was ceding the centre ground, something Morawiecki, who represents the more moderate, technocratic side of PiS, was particularly concerned about (alongside his own waning influence). When in power, PiS launched a revolution in Poland's energy transition. But now, in opposition, it has disowned those achievements and returned to an emphasis on coal. This could be a missed opportunity to win back centrist voters, writes @OrzelBartlomiej https://t.co/8cGvubn7N2 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 29, 2026 Should Morawiecki now, as expected, launch his own centre-right party, focused on economic development, it would appeal to moderate conservatives who are opposed to the Tusk government but put off by the far right and PiS’s own hardline turn. Inevitably, some of the support for Development Plus would come at the expense of PiS – but not all of it, and possibly not even most of it. An example of something similar happening can be seen elsewhere among the opposition. Until last year, KKP was part of Confederation. However, its leader, Grzegorz Braun, was expelled after announcing a run for the presidency against Confederation’s official candidate, Sławomir Mentzen. In June 2025, KKP formed its own parliamentary caucus. Since then, support for Confederation has remained stable at around 13-14%, while KKP has risen to over 9% in the polls. So, by splitting, the two groups actually increased the size of their potential electorate, with KKP successfully appealing to an even more radical pool of voters than Confederation. It is possible that Morawiecki could do the same in the opposite direction – his new party winning over moderate conservatives while PiS continues to appeal to its most loyal supporters as well as competing with the far right. There certainly seems to be fertile ground for such a party. Regular polling by the state research agency CBOS shows that the proportion of Poles with a negative view of Tusk’s government rose to its joint-highest level this month, at 48%, while only 29% have a positive view. The last time that positive views outnumbered negative ones was in February 2024, the second full month of the current ruling coalition’s time in power. Among those who voted for Tusk and his allies in 2023, dissatisfaction is strongest among moderate conservatives. Both Tusk’s centrist KO and one of his coalition partners, The Left (Lewica), are polling only slightly below the proportion of votes they received in that year (30.7% and 8.6%, respectively). However, the most conservative part of the coalition, the centre-right Third Way (Trzecia Droga) alliance, has fallen from 14.4% of the vote in 2023 to only around 4-5% today for the two parties that constituted it, Poland 2050 (Polska 2050) and the Polish People’s Party (PSL) (which last year decided to go their separate ways). An IBRiS poll for Polsat News in April this year found that, whereas 84% of KO voters and 57.1% of Left voters have a positive view of Tusk’s government, that figure falls to 42.5% for Third Way voters, a majority of whom (51.6%) have a negative opinion. PSL and Poland 2050, the two parties that make up the Third Way alliance, have confirmed that they are splitting and will stand separately at the next elections. They will, however, remain part of @donaldtusk's ruling coalition https://t.co/NduEJY25eE — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 18, 2025 Moderate conservatives’ disillusionment with the government, combined with PiS’s shift away from the centre ground, gives a clear opportunity for Morawiecki. And Tusk’s coalition itself showed in 2023 the advantages for the opposition in offering a broader set of options. While some – in KO in particular – had pushed for centrist and left-wing parties to stand jointly on a single list at that year’s elections, instead they campaigned as three main blocs. That gave voters opposed to the PiS government a genuine choice, and likely played a big part in the record turnout that helped bring Tusk’s coalition to power. It is similarly possible now that a four-branched opposition, ranging from Morawiecki on the centre right, through PiS and Confederation, to Braun on the radical right, could together win a parliamentary majority. Polls currently show those four groups with combined support of around 50% (though polling regarding support for Morawiecki’s prospective party should for now be treated with caution). Jestem dumny z tego, co wspólnie zrobiliśmy dla Polski. I wiem jedno – nasza misja wciąż trwa💪🇵🇱#RozwojPlus pic.twitter.com/xOnxKDoroS — Mateusz Morawiecki (@MorawieckiM) July 31, 2026 However, even if they do win a majority, it is far from certain what would happen then. In 2023, the three opposition blocs were, although standing separately, clearly aligned with one another and focused on removing PiS from power. When they together won a parliamentary majority, it was absolutely clear they would form a coalition government. By contrast, today’s opposition is deeply divided. Confederation and KKP regularly attack PiS. It is not at all clear that Confederation would be willing to form a coalition government with PiS, while Kaczyński has explicitly ruled out working with the pro-Russian, anti-American Braun. Meanwhile, Morawiecki’s split has followed months of bitter infighting within PiS, which has often been carried out in public. The manner in which he and his allies are now departing the party means that relations with PiS are likely to remain difficult. The national-conservative opposition PiS party's newly named candidate for prime minister has made overtures to the far-right Confederation. But he also ruled out Grzegorz Braun, an even more radical far-right figure, serving in a PiS-led government https://t.co/i3zOZJWdUN — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 9, 2026 It would therefore be hard for the opposition to form a government, even if they do win a majority. In this situation, the role of President Karol Nawrocki may be vital. Though elected with the support of PiS last year, he was technically an independent and maintained good relations with Confederation and even, to some extent, Braun (who endorsed Nawrocki after being eliminated in the first round). When Morawiecki this week announced the “ten pillars” of Development Plus’s programme, he made clear his loyalty to Nawrocki: the second of those pillars is “respect for the president”. Nie ma silnej Polski bez wielkich ambicji. Nie ma wielkich ambicji bez ludzi, którzy je zdefiniują i będą gotowi wziąć odpowiedzialność za ich realizację. Bezpieczeństwo. Rozwój. Suwerenność. Ambicja. Tożsamość. Patriotyzm. To nie hasła wyborcze, ale fundamenty państwa, które… pic.twitter.com/G0YBbfhLye — Mateusz Morawiecki (@MorawieckiM) July 28, 2026 Many on the right hope that Nawrocki can play a role next year in helping the opposition present a more united front during the election campaign. It is also the president who decides who gets the opportunity to try to form a government after the elections. That role would be of particular significance if, as is very possible, Tusk’s KO emerges as the biggest individual party but the opposition together may be able to form a parliamentary majority. Given that we are still over 14 months away from the elections, and Morawiecki has not even yet officially split from PiS, it is still far too early to make confident predictions. However, while Morawiecki’s likely departure is clearly a personal blow to Kaczyński – and a sign of the 77-year-old’s waning influence over not only the Polish right but even his own party – it may conversely provide a boost to the opposition as a whole. Poland has banned children from using smartphones and other electronic devices in primary schools and kindergartens in a bid to improve their wellbeing and safety. The new legislation, signed into law by opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki on Thursday, will take effect at the start of the school year on 1 September, but schools will have until the end of 2026 to adjust. Prezydent podpisał nowelizację, która zakazuje korzystania z telefonów komórkowych w przedszkolach i szkołach. (PAP)#PAPInformacje pic.twitter.com/CK7YFU7sru — Polska Agencja Prasowa/Polish Press Agency (PAP) (@PAPinformacje) July 30, 2026 Under the new rules, pupils in primary schools and kindergartens will be prohibited from using smartphones and other electronic devices allowing communication or audio and video recording for the entire school day, including breaks and lessons held outside of school grounds. Schools will be allowed, but not required, to create designated places where pupils’ devices can be stored in a safe way and with respect for their privacy. The law, however, allows for some exceptions. When pupils need a device because of illness, disability or other special needs, school headteachers can permit their use. Phones could also be used in emergencies where there is a direct threat to life, health or property. Furthermore, pupils will be permitted to use mobile phones if a teacher deems them necessary for educational purposes and gives approval. The law also allows secondary schools to introduce bans on smartphone use if they choose, but does not make this compulsory, with such schools retaining autonomy to set their own rules through their statutes. The draft law banning phones from primary schools was first approved by the government in June. It then went to the Sejm, the lower and more powerful chamber of Poland’s parliament, which introduced amendments, including extending the measures to kindergartens. The Sejm then approved the bill in a rare near-unanimous vote, with only some MPs from the far-right Confederation (Konfederacja) voting against it. Subsequently, the Senate passed the bill without amendments, sending it to Nawrocki, who could have signed it, vetoed it, or sent it to Poland’s constitutional court for review. Poland’s government has approved a ban on mobile phones in primary schools as well as tougher age-verification requirements for online pornography. Both measures still require parliamentary and presidential approval before becoming law https://t.co/y4Ycf46FQD — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 2, 2026 The president ultimately decided to sign the law, with his office noting that the measures aim to “create safer learning conditions” and support the “healthy and responsible” use of digital technologies by pupils. Poland’s education minister Barbara Nowacka said last month that the law would “improve teachers’ power, autonomy and agency, as well as order and digital wellbeing in schools”. She added that, although many schools already have such bans in place, teachers had asked for legal backing to help enforce them. For more on the measures, see our earlier report from when the bill was approved almost unanimously by parliament, with only the far right voting against it https://t.co/9Mx0SfkE5V — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 17, 2026 According to a survey conducted in April by the Polish state research institute CBOS for the Polish Press Agency (PAP), 85% of Poles support a ban on the use of smartphones in primary schools. Poland has been recently stepping up efforts to protect young people from various digital threats. The topic has been a rare area of consensus between the government and Nawrocki, who has vetoed a record number of bills. Earlier this month, Nawrocki signed a law banning online content depicting illegal acts or other forms of abusive and degrading behaviour – known in Polish as “patostreaming”. Another measure approved by the government that is now being considered by parliament is the introduction of stricter age-verification requirements for accessing online pornography. In January, the digital affairs ministry also announced that it hoped to introduce measures blocking children from access to social media. Poland hopes this year to introduce measures preventing children from accessing social media, says the country's digital affairs ministry. It is working on tools that would require platforms to verify the age of users https://t.co/G7qeEl2q9x — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 5, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. Polish authorities have confirmed that the object that violated Polish airspace and crashed in eastern Poland was a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile carrying a significant explosive payload. The missile entered Poland during a period of intensive overnight Russian attacks on Ukraine, travelling around 100 km over Polish territory before exploding in a field in the Lublin region on Thursday morning. Nie miejmy żadnych złudzeń. Tego typu sytuacje albo tego typu prowokacje będą się zdarzać – powiedział wiceminister obrony Cezary Tomczyk w @faktypofaktach, komentując wybuch rakiety na Lubelszczyźnie.https://t.co/IKxuGNwe05 — tvn24 (@tvn24) July 30, 2026 “We can confidently confirm that it was a Russian Kh-101 missile, a cruise missile capable of carrying even nuclear warheads, which exploded on impact,” deputy defence minister Cezary Tomczyk told broadcaster TVN24 late on Thursday. The object was “a potentially very dangerous missile,” Tomczyk added. Asked whether the incident could have been a deliberate move by Moscow, he said that no possibilities could be ruled out. “We don’t know, and if we do find out, it will mainly be through intelligence. I’m sure the coming weeks will provide us with more answers,” the deputy minister said. Tomczyk said Poland was working closely with Ukraine, adding that 20 of the roughly 70 missiles fired by Russia overnight from Wednesday to Thursday were at one point heading towards Poland. “It is also worth noting that the vast majority of these missiles were shot down by Ukraine over Ukrainian territory, which clearly bore the full brunt of the attack,” he said. He added that a Ukrainian pilot had tracked the missile that later fell on Polish territory but was unable to intercept it. “He turned back 20 seconds before reaching the border,” Tomczyk said, adding that the pilot “could not have flown into” Polish airspace. An object crashed into a field 100 km from Poland’s border with Ukraine overnight after a major Russian attack. Ukrainian officials said it was a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile, while Poland reported an "extremely difficult night for our air defence"https://t.co/QIpRQfej5S — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 30, 2026 Prosecutors who concluded their work at the site on Thursday said the missile contained a “significant amount of explosive material”. Investigators collected fragments and soil samples from the impact site, where the explosion left a crater around 10 metres wide and 5 metres deep. “The crater has been filled and the site handed back to its owner. The Territorial Defence Force combed through an area of approximately 3 km² and found numerous rocket debris, including propulsion components,” the Lublin prosecutor’s office said. Prokuratorzy właśnie zakończyli swoje czynności na miejscu zdarzenia. Lej został zasypany, a teren przekazany właścicielowi. WOT przeczesał teren o powierzchni ok 3 km2 znajdując liczne szczątki rakiety w tym elementy napędu. — Prokuratura Okręgowa w Lublinie (@Prok_Okreg_Lub) July 30, 2026 The incident came amid a political dispute in Poland over its air-defence capabilities. Earlier this month, the government confirmed it had transferred PAC-3 missiles for Patriot systems to Ukraine, prompting opposition criticism that the move had weakened Poland’s defences. Following the latest incident, Prime Minister Donald Tusk said the government would, paradoxically, consider providing Ukraine with further military aid, including additional Patriot air-defence systems if necessary. “Our intention is to ensure that Ukraine does not lose this war,” Tusk said. The Polish government has confirmed that it has transferred Patriot missiles to Ukraine following opposition criticism It also released a list of all military donations to Ukraine since 2022, showing that the former PiS government gave much more equipment https://t.co/8BmDy5BjiB — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 7, 2026 The incident also prompted reactions from NATO allies and other world leaders. The US ambassador to Poland, Thomas Rose, said that Washington was in close contact with Polish authorities and NATO allies following the incident. “Any breach of a NATO ally’s territory is a matter we take extremely seriously,” Rose wrote on X. “We are coordinating closely with Polish authorities as the investigation proceeds and remain committed to defending Allied territory and upholding NATO’s collective security.” We are in constant contact with the Government of Poland —including @KosiniakKamysz @sikorskiradek @marcin_przydacz @CTomczyk and @POTUS @usambnato Matt Whitaker following this morning’s violation of Polish airspace by a Russian fired projectile that impacted deep inside Polish… — Ambassador Tom Rose (@USAmbPoland) July 30, 2026 NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte called the incident “yet another reckless act by Russia and a dangerous consequence of its war against Ukraine”. He said that NATO would continue to strengthen its readiness to defend against all threats. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz condemned the the attacks on Ukraine, saying that the violation of Polish airspace that accompanied them demonstrated “Russian ruthlessness and readiness to escalate”. Johann Wadephul, Germany’s foreign minister, said the violations of Polish and Romanian airspace showed that Russia remained “the greatest threat to our security”. He reaffirmed Berlin’s support for Ukraine, as well as European Union and NATO allies. Wir verurteilen die massiven russischen Angriffe auf die Ukraine scharf. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland will deport a Colombian citizen who performed a Nazi salute during his visit to the former German-Nazi death camp of Auschwitz-Birkenau. He is banned from re-entering Poland and the Schengen area for five years. The 34-year-old was charged with promoting Nazism, an offence carrying a maximum sentence of three years in prison, and desecration of a memorial site. “A place that symbolises one of the greatest tragedies in human history requires special respect, and insulting it does not go without consequences,” said the border guard. @PolskaPolicja zatrzymała ob. Kolumbii 🇨🇴, który na terenie Muzeum Auschwitz-Birkenau propagował nazizm i znieważył miejsce pamięci. Komendant #PlacówkaSGwKrakowie wydał wobec cudzoziemca decyzję o zobowiązaniu do powrotu oraz 5-letni zakaz wjazdu do 🇵🇱 i państw strefy Schengen. pic.twitter.com/kzfw1Kzw8w — Straż Graniczna (@Straz_Graniczna) July 30, 2026 Police in Oświęcim, the town where the museum is located, said in mid-July that they had detained a man after being notified by museum guards of a possible offence. A police probe found that the man, who had been living and working in the Wielkopolska province, had “posed for a photo making the Nazi salute” at the museum while visiting it. Prosecutors were informed of the case, police said, adding that the man was subsequently charged with two crimes: public promotion of Nazism and the desecration of a memorial site. He admitted to the offences and voluntarily submitted to his punishment, which consisted of a 2,000 zloty (€464) fine along with a decision for his verdict to be made public, they added. He was then handed over to Poland’s border guard, which decided to deport him and ban him from entering Poland and other Schengen countries for five years. The border guard said that the decision was “immediately enforceable”, and was based on “considerations of security and public order as well as the interests of the Republic of Poland.” It also noted that a court decided to place the man in a facility for foreigners in the city of Przemyśl, where he will await deportation. Polish prosecutors have indicted an Iranian-born German citizen for making statements denying the Holocaust during a tour of Auschwitz, which he then published in an online video Denying Nazi crimes carries a prison sentence of up to three years in Poland https://t.co/WCSm7O4gAx — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 4, 2026 The Auschwitz Museum has in recent years dealt with various cases of visitors misbehaving, including in ways that are punishable by law. Earlier this month, prosecutors in Poland indicted an Iranian-born German citizen for making statements denying the Holocaust during a tour of Auschwitz. In 2025, an Israeli teenager who was seen doing a fascist salute at the former German-Nazi camp was fined for propagating Nazism. Auschwitz was first set up by Nazi Germany in occupied Poland in 1940 during World War Two as a camp to house Polish “political” prisoners, before later becoming primarily a site for the murder of Jews. At least 1.3 million victims were transported there, with at least 1.1 million of them killed at the camp. Around one million of those victims were Jews. The second largest group of victims – around 70,000 people – were ethnic Poles. On the 80th anniversary of the liberation of Auschwitz, we look at the extraordinary story of Anna Odi, who has lived her entire life in the grounds of the former concentration camp as the daughter of survivors who helped establish the @AuschwitzMuseum https://t.co/d2enYJRjMk — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 27, 2025 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. Poland’s government has appointed a marketing and branding expert to develop a unified strategy for promoting the country abroad, saying the move will help boost tourism, support Polish products and attract foreign investment. Barbara Mróz-Gorgoń, a professor at Wrocław University of Economics, noted that her appointment signals “a shift” from simple promotional activities to “managing the reputation of our great country”. The move comes as Poland seeks to capitalise on its economic success, including growth in tourism and continued investments. But the government says that current promotion efforts lack a single strategy and are fragmented. Czas na markę Polska! Witamy na pokładzie prof. Barbarę Mróz – Gorgoń 🇵🇱 pic.twitter.com/PPX2eWTRSm — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) July 29, 2026 Last year, Poland’s sport and tourism ministry appointed Mróz-Gorgoń, who also advises companies and institutions on branding strategy and founded a think tank dedicated to promoting Poland, to an interministerial team tasked with developing a comprehensive new branding strategy for Poland. The government said, however, that efforts to promote Poland were so far fragmented and lacked a single strategy, which is why it created the post of commissioner for promotion of the Poland brand. As the first specialist to take the position, Mróz-Gorgoń will be tasked with preparing a strategy to build a national brand and help implement it, coordinate activities to help grow tourism, support investments, and improve Poland’s position on the world stage. “We will create one programme resulting in the joint promotion of our country’s brand,” said Tusk. According to the government, this will come at no further cost, but ensure that existing funds will be spent in a more “coherent and effective way”. Mróz-Gorgoń, meanwhile, noted that “the Poland brand is not the property of the government. It is created by entrepreneurs, artists, athletes, local governments and millions of Poles at home and abroad”. Developing this brand “means more investment, recognition of our brands and products abroad, and it also provides greater strength in international relations,” she continued. Poland saw the EU's second-fastest growth in tourism in 2025, behind only the Mediterranean island state of Malta https://t.co/WVkRbHtU7o — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 19, 2026 Poland has been one of the world’s fastest-growing economies in recent decades. The growth has coincided with the international expansion of its firms, more foreign investments, and a rapidly expanding tourism sector. Last year, the sport and tourism ministry announced that it wants tourism to contribute 9% of GDP annually within a decade, from about 5% now, and for Poland to become a leader in the sector in central and eastern Europe. Foreign direct investment in Poland grew from just under 15.5 billion zloty in 2003, a year before the country joined the European Union, to around 61.3 billion zloty last year, according to figures from the National Bank of Poland (NBP). Various state and private companies – such as delivery giant InPost, insurer PZU, and train manufacturer Pesa – are establishing themselves abroad by buying some of their rivals. The international success of some Polish athletes – including football player Robert Lewandowski and tennis star Iga Świątek – has also helped improve Poland’s visibility. Prime Minister Donald Tusk said on Thursday that Polish airspace had been violated during a massive missile attack by Russia on western Ukraine overnight, adding that there were no casualties or immediate threat to civilians. A suspected Russian Kh-101 cruise missile crashed in eastern Poland, around 100 km from the Ukrainian border, prompting the deployment of police counter-terrorism officers and other security services to the site. The fall of the object, which is reported to have caused a powerful explosion, left a crater about 10 metres wide and scattered fragments in a field between Tarnawa-Kolonia and Tokary in Lublin province, about 2 km from the nearest buildings, according to local police. TYLKO U NAS! Wybuch i ogromny krater na #Lubelszczyźnie. Mamy zdjęcia! >> https://t.co/BrX7XneP7F Fot. Radio ESKA pic.twitter.com/BgzlhpSVag — ESKA (@eska_pl) July 30, 2026 Lublin prosecutor Grzegorz Trusiewicz told reporters at the site of the incident that the crater was about 5 metres deep and that fragments had been scattered across an area of roughly 200 metres. Ukraine has offered Poland assistance in investigating the scene, he added. Earlier in the morning, Poland’s Armed Forces Operational Command (DORSZ) said that air defence radars had detected at least a dozen missiles over western Ukraine overnight whose trajectories could have posed a potential threat to Polish airspace. An unidentified object was detected in Polish airspace at 3:40 a.m. travelling westward, DORSZ said. An F-16 fighter jet was dispatched to identify and intercept it. At 3:46 a.m., before the object could be clearly identified, it disappeared from the radar. An Mi-24 helicopter was then sent to the area of the last radar detection to verify the indications. Its crew located what was believed to be the crash site. W trakcie rosyjskiego zmasowanego ataku rakietowego na zachodnią Ukrainę doszło do naruszenia polskiej przestrzeni powietrznej. Zwołałem w związku z tym zespół koordynacyjny z udziałem Ministra Obrony i odpowiednich służb, które od wielu godzin pracują na miejscu zdarzenia i… — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) July 30, 2026 Tusk said the initial information suggested the object was likely a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile, echoing earlier comments made by Ukraine’s acting foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, but stressed that investigators would need to establish the precise type and origin of the object. “We will want to be 100% certain: what kind of missile, who launched it, whether it was the explosion of the payload or the impact of the missile itself that caused this crater,” he said at a press conference in Lublin. The prime minister added that Polish forces had been prepared to shoot down the object had it continued flying in a way that posed a threat. Tusk added that another missile approached the Polish border but did not enter Polish airspace. “This initial information clearly indicates that the relevant services, the military, our pilots, and our aircraft acted very quickly and efficiently. There was no immediate threat due to the missile falling in an undeveloped area,” Tusk said. He added that he had discussed the incident with opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki. An early warning system was activated in Lublin and several other areas of the province because of Russian air attacks on Ukraine. The alarm lasted about 13 minutes, according to the interior minister. The opposition criticised the authorities for not providing residents with further information about the reason for the alarm. “A few minutes of alarm, no information in the mainstream media about what was happening, some residents didn’t even hear the sirens, and no text messages with an alert from the Government Centre for Security (RCB),” wrote Michał Dworczyk, a Law and Justice (PiS) MP, on social media. World.title: Record number of Poles opposed to Ukraine’s EU membership
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Support for Ukraine joining the European Union has fallen sharply in Poland, with opposition reaching a record high of 40%, a survey carried out by the Polish state research agency CBOS shows. The figures show that 50% of Poles still support Ukraine’s EU membership, but that is a significant decline from 74% in October 2023, when the question was last asked, and from a record 90% in March 2022, shortly after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The shift comes as public sentiment towards Ukrainians in general in Poland has deteriorated in recent years. The latest CBOS poll shows that, among those who support Ukraine’s EU accession, most favour a gradual process, with 41% of all respondents saying Ukraine should join the EU but “without undue haste”. “Only 9% of respondents currently support Ukraine’s earliest possible EU membership, which is the lowest figure in the history of these surveys,” CBOS reported. Meanwhile, opposition to Ukraine’s EU membership has increased by 23 percentage points since October 2023, reaching its highest level in the history of CBOS surveys. People with right-wing political beliefs are most likely to be opposed to Ukraine’s accession (53%), while the age group with the highest percentage of people opposed is those aged 18-24 (58%). The survey also found that a majority of Poles expect the war in Ukraine to end with territorial concessions from Kyiv – 55% of respondents said they believed Ukraine would lose some territory, a view that has remained dominant since December 2024. Compared with the previous survey, however, pessimism has eased. The proportion of respondents who expect Ukraine to lose part of its territory fell by 8 percentage points, while the number expecting Russia to take control of the entire country declined from 8% to 6%. On Western support for Ukraine, 39% of respondents said the military, financial and humanitarian assistance provided by countries in the West was sufficient. Meanwhile, 27% said aid was excessive, while 22% said it was insufficient. Russia has published purported archival documents relating to massacres of Poles by Ukrainians in WWII. Kyiv had warned that Russia was planning to release the files in order to stir tensions, while Polish media note that the material contains nothing new https://t.co/CI0cfAlDle — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 6, 2026 Ukrainians are Poland’s largest foreign national group, with almost 1.6 million living in the country, but recent polls have shown growing hostility towards them, fuelled in part by anti-Ukrainian rhetoric from far-right parties and a tougher stance towards Kyiv from some opposition politicians. In its annual survey of attitudes towards national and ethnic groups, CBOS found earlier this year that the proportion of Poles who said they disliked Ukrainians increased by five percentage points this year, the largest rise recorded among all groups surveyed, reaching 43%. Tensions between the two countries have also been heightened by disputes over historical issues and a series of recent incidents targeting Ukrainians in Poland. The number of reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland is up 30% so far this year, police data show. The figures come following recent high-profile cases of verbal and physical attacks against Ukrainians, who are Poland's largest immigrant group https://t.co/pcTsJddDz7 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 17, 2026 The number of reported hate crimes against Ukrainians rose by 30% in the first half of 2026 compared with the same period a year earlier, according to newly reported police data. Last weekend, three men were filmed violently attacking a Ukrainian woman and her partner outside a shop in Wrocław, apparently because of her accent. Two of the assailants have since been detained by police, while their victims required treatment in hospital. In response, Prime Minister Donald Tusk called for Poles to “wage war on violence”, saying that the perpetrators of such acts “have become emboldened precisely because they now have political role models, political patrons, and political support”.
